Documents: Page 1 of 1 TOWN OF BOW Planning Board 10 Grandview Road, Bow, New Hampshire 03304 Phone (603) 223-3976 | Fax (603) 225-2982 | Website www.bownh.gov NOTICE OF PUBLIC HEARING Planning Board Town of Bow Notice is hereby given in accordance with NH RSA 675:7, that a public hearing will be conducted pursuant to RSA 675:3 at 7:00 PM on Thursday, December 3, 2026 at the Bow High School Auditorium, 55 Falcon Way to consider placing the following on the Town Warrant: A.

To adopt a Temporary Moratorium on Large Resource-Consuming Uses Ordinance pursuant to RSA 674:23 If approved, this moratorium would prohibit Large Resource-Consuming Uses (LRCUs) throughout the town for period of one year. As more specifically defined in the ordinance, LRCUs are those commercial and industrial uses that consume designated amounts of electricity and water and include but are not limited to data centers, heavy manufacturing facilities, electric generating facilities, oil or gas refineries, natural gas storage facilities, and regional warehouse distribution centers.

The text of the proposed ordinance is available for review on the Town website and at the Bow Community Development Office. You may attend this meeting for the purpose of presenting your comments on any action the Planning Board may take concerning this proposed ordinance. If you have any questions, please contact Karri Makinen, Community Development Director at (603) 223-3971. TEMPORARY MORATORIUM ON LARGE RESOURCE- CONSUMING USES ORDINANCE Pursuant to RSA 674:23 I. Title This ordinance shall be known as the “Temporary Moratorium on Large Resource-Consuming Uses Ordinance.” This Ordinance shall be referenced herein as “the Ordinance.” II.

Authority This ordinance is adopted under the authority of RSA 674:23, which permits municipalities to adopt temporary interim zoning ordinances to preserve the status quo pending the development and adoption of permanent zoning ordinance or other land use regulations when unusual circumstances may affect a municipality’s ability to provide adequate services and requires prompt attention to develop a zoning ordinance. III. Determination of Unusual Circumstances In adopting this Ordinance, the voters of the Town of Bow hereby determine as follows: A. WHEREAS, the Town of Bow was previously the host community to the Merrimack Station Coal-Fired Power Plant; B.

WHEREAS, in 2024, the Merrimack Station Coal-Fired Power Plant retired and is no longer in operation; C. WHEREAS, the retirement of the Merrimack Station Coal-Fired Power Plant has called into question potential uses for the former site of the power plant, the use of electric utility infrastructure and other resources in the Town previously utilized by the Merrimack Station Coal-Fired Power Plant, and the potential for certain Large Resource-Consuming Uses to be proposed in the Town; D.

WHEREAS, Large Resource-Consuming Uses (“LRCUs”), including, but not limited to data centers, represent a new and rapidly expanding form of industrial land use that is not specifically addressed in the Town’s current Zoning Ordinance; E. THEREFORE, unusual circumstances exist in the Town of Bow that may affect the ability of the Town of Bow to provide adequate services and, due to the potential for a Large Resource-Consuming Use to enter the Town of Bow, prompt attention is needed to develop a zoning ordinance and other land use regulations regarding such uses. IV. Purpose and Intent The purpose of this Ordinance is to: A.

Protect the public health, safety, and welfare of the residents of Bow, protect against adverse regional impacts, ensure the availability and reliability of electrical supply, ensure adequate access to potable drinking water, safeguard the regional watershe

Town of Bow Buildings & Facilities Advisory Committee Meeting DRAFT November 17, 2026 Present: David Cook (Chair), Thomas Betteridge (Vice Chair & Secretary), Glenn Dugas 1. Call to order. a. David Cook (Chair) Called meeting to order at 6:07 pm. 2. Public Comment a. None 3. Acceptance of the minutes a. Motion to approve the 6/2/2026 meeting minutes by Glenn Dugas, second by David Cook. Unanimous approval. 4. New business: a. Review of Committee Charge: • Assess and analyze municipally owned buildings and facilities in order to prioritize physical plant needs and budgets.

• Develop a facilities assessment and analysis methodology and process that informs decision makers and enables priority setting among Capital Improvement Program (CIP), replacement, renovation, and maintenance projects. • Advise the Bord of Selectmen, Town Manager, and Building and Facilities Manager, on building and facilities priorities, including construction, replacement, renovation and maintenance and the development of an overall facilities strategy. b. The committee feels they have developed a good database / plan for the municipally owned buildings and facilities to allow for projects to be priorities with appropriate budgets put fourth to the CIP committee.

• The committee feels they can work on adjusting the items being put forth to the CIP committee in 2 or 3 meetings each year since the basis for the buildings has been established. c. The committee discussed that they could do more to support some of the future planning for the different facilities and buildings within the town. For example, the Municipal building parking lot and building itself, the committee has made some recommendations, but a larger discussion on the future use of the building, what other options there are to shift sport events, etc. need to be discussed or direction needs to be provided by the selectboard. d.

The committee is going to request a meeting or discussion with the selectboard to better understand how we can help support them and the town with the overall facility strategies. 5. Old business: a. Library: None b. Safety Center Update: None c. Municipal Building: None d. Hanson Park Update: None e. DPW Update:. None f. Old Town Hall Update: None g. Rec Center Update: None h. Budget Update: None i. Community building Update: None j. Town wide update: None k. Other: 6. Next meeting date and location a. 01/05/2027 at 6 pm Location, Municipal building. 7. Adjourn a. Motion to adjourn by Glenn Dugas seconded by David Cook. Unanimously approved. The meeting was adjourned at 6:28 pm.

Town of Bow Recycling and Solid Waste Committee November 10, 2026 Meeting Draft Meeting Minutes To:​ David Stack, Town Manager cc:​ Bow Administrative Assistant, Committee Webpage, Recycling Committee Members Re: ​ Recycling and Solid Waste Committee Minutes for November 10, 2026 Meeting (DRAFT) Date:​ November 10, 2026 Committee Member Attendees: Sherri Cheney, Deb Unger, Beth Titus, and Irene Hou. Other Attendees: Greg Rule Dunbarton Transfer Station Manager MEETING BEGAN AT 7:15 P.M. 1.​ Review of October 6, 2026 Meeting Minutes Motion by Sherri Cheney to approve October 6, 2026 draft minutes, seconded by Beth Titus, unanimously approved.

2.​ Recycling Tipping Fees –Rates Sherri Cheney reported on tipping fees for recyclables. The tipping fee for October was $141.35 per ton. 3. ​ Recycling and Solid Waste Totals Sherri reported on collection amounts for single stream recycling and solid waste for October. Recycling was 64.54 tons and trash was 177.69 tons. 4. Facebook Page Update Irene was unable to obtain administration access to the Town of Bow facebook page despite communicating with Mark and Tonia. There was a discussion about starting a new page, but it was then decided that we would ask Tonia to occasionally post for us pending Mark’s return to the committee. 5.

Renewal Garden and Compost Update The compost program continues to run smoothly and be well used. 6. Status of Terracycle Containers Irene reported that she has submitted one box of snack pouches, totaling 1488 points ($14.88), since the last meeting. She plans to submit a box of trigger heads this week. She also updated the signage to reflect that the juice pouch program has been discontinued and will store the extra container for future replacement needs. 7. 2026 HOUSEHOLD HAZARDOUS WASTE DAY UPDATE Sherri reported there were a total of 395 cars which was 16% fewer cars than 2025, but still 3% more cars than our prior 18 year average.

This included 319 cars from Bow, 70 from Dunbarton and 6 with electronics only. The residency check went smoothly. For improvements, Deb mentioned that the entrance sign could be improved as there were some cars that needed to turn around to enter. Deb also recommended that cones could be used to better coordinate 2 lanes of vehicles at the beginning of the line. There was a discussion about how the post-it notes worked. It was discussed that a washable car window marker could communicate the same information, but would be cheaper and easier for next year. Greg Rule reported that Dunbarton’s collection of local items went well.

He submitted to Sherri the total amounts for the local items, with the exception of small propane containers which he plans to bring to North Coast Services. The cost of U-Haul rental including gas was $111.75 total, which was less than last year. The vendor charge from NH Recycles was $25,214.20 ($4800 Set up Free, $34 per unit cost, 533 total units, plus a $2292.20 for a 10% Energy, Assurance and Compliance Fee.) Sherri reported that the waste oil collection went smoothly. The NHDES Grant report is due January 15th, 2027. Sherri is collecting the invoices and Greg will forward the final Dunbarton bills as soon as he completes them.

Deb will write up a description of the educational components and email it to Sherri for the Grant report. Irene offered to assist Sherri in completing the report once all the information has been collected. Sherri suggested reaching out to the BHS Environmental Club to assist with volunteers at next year’s HHWD. 8. Trex Program: Plastic bag and Film Collection The program and collection have been working well. At the last meeting, Heath stated he put together the bench and he would contact Darcy Little to arrange placement at the Bow Rec Center Before/After School program building. 9.​ HELPSY Helpsy collected 715 pounds for the July-September period. The October collection was 169 pounds.

10. Other business Sherri updated our committee’s activities at the Joint Meeting with the Board of Selectmen and Town Committees on October 13th. Irene attended as well. Deb offered to reach out to the new Stroll magazine to see if they would do an article on our committee to educate the public. Deb also offered to reach out to Nadine at the Bow Times to do an article every 2 months for public education. Next Committee meeting is January 5, 2027. Meeting adjourned at 8:27 p.m. Respectfully Submitted, Irene Hou

Review of Potential Zoning Amendments 16 Chairman Berube recognized Lyn Lull and Lynne Powers, speaking on behalf of a group of residents who 17 submitted a petition containing approximately 826 signatures requesting consideration of a temporary 18 one-year moratorium on data center development. Ms.

Powers stated that the petition and supporting 19 materials had been submitted to Town Hall and requested that the Planning Board recommend a special 20 Town Meeting and warrant article addressing a temporary moratorium. 21 Selectman McDaniel summarized legal guidance received from Town Counsel regarding the petitioned 22 data center moratorium. He explained that, pursuant to the applicable RSA, only the Planning Board may 23 recommend a zoning moratorium, while the Select Board's role is limited to calling a special meeting.

He 24 further noted that a moratorium must satisfy specific statutory requirements, including findings of unusual 25 circumstances and a defined plan of study or corrective action during the moratorium period. Selectman 26 McDaniel stated that, while the petition containing 826 signatures demonstrated significant public 27 interest, it was advisory in nature and did not have binding legal effect on the Planning Board. He also 28 explained that once a public hearing is posted for a proposed moratorium or zoning amendment, statutory 29 protections are triggered that prevent applicants from locking in existing regulations before the matter can 30 be considered. Mr.

McDaniel noted that the Town had already begun reviewing potential ordinance 31 amendments related to large energy-consuming uses, including draft provisions addressing noise 32 standards, third-party review requirements, and other potential impacts. He stated that the Board would 33 need to determine whether to proceed with a temporary moratorium, continue development of ordinance 34 amendments, or pursue both approaches concurrently, and indicated that a public hearing could be 35 scheduled for the Board's December meeting. 36 Ms.

Powers, a resident of Hooksett working with Bow residents on the petition effort, thanked staff for 37 relaying Town Counsel's feedback regarding the proposed moratorium. She explained that the petitioners 38 proceeded using the RSA they believed was applicable at the time and noted that the draft moratorium 39 ordinance submitted to the Board was modeled after an ordinance previously adopted by the Town of 40 Nottingham. Ms. Powers stated that the draft includes a process and framework intended to address 41 concerns regarding the scope and implementation of a moratorium.

She further advised that petition 42 organizers had received differing guidance from individuals involved with the Nottingham ordinance 43 effort, including discussions with the New Hampshire Municipal Association and legal counsel, who 44 indicated that moving forward with such a proposal may be permissible under state law. 45 During Board discussion, members considered whether work on a temporary moratorium and the 46 development of zoning ordinance amendments could proceed simultaneously.

Selectman McDaniel stated 47 that, if a moratorium were pursued, the Board would continue researching issues associated with large 48 energy-consuming uses, including noise impacts, water usage, and regulatory approaches adopted by 49 other municipalities, while also evaluating potential amendments to the Town's zoning ordinance. 50 Ms. Lull raised a question regarding how the Town evaluates potential project impacts. Ms. Makinen 51 noted that all development applications are reviewed for potential regional impacts and stated that a data 52 center proposal would likely have significant regional implications. Chair Berube Jr.

explained that, when 53 technical issues such as traffic, drainage, or noise require specialized analysis, the Town retains 54 independent third-party consultants, selected by the Town and funded by the applicant, to review and 55 provide expert findings. Ms. Lull expressed concern that certain potential impacts associated with data 56 centers, including effects related to noise and animal welfare, may not yet be fully understood or 57 researched and questioned whether adequate information would be available to evaluate such impacts. 58 Board members acknowledged that the scope and nature of any required expert review would depend on 59 the specifics of a future application.

60 Susan Moore, 11 Crockett Drive, expressed concern that any future ordinance addressing data center 61 noise should consider not only decibel levels but also low-frequency noise. She stated that research has 62 associated low-frequency noise with potential health impacts and emphasized the importance of 63 evaluating those effects when developing regulatory standards. 64 Ms. Lull asked about coordination between municipalities on issues related to data center development. 65 Ms. Makinen indicated that communities routinely share information and that other municipalities had 66 already reached out to Bow regarding its ongoing discussions.

Selectman McDaniel noted that any future 67 data center proposal would receive extensive public review and technical evaluation and emphasized that 68 all Planning Board proceedings are conducted in public session except as permitted by law. 69 Ms. Makinen further reported that staff had begun seeking acoustic engineering professionals to obtain 70 expert feedback and assist the Board in evaluating potential noise regulations. 71 Selectman McDaniel questioned whether a moratorium could discourage potential applications while the 72 Town studies the issue and develops regulatory standards.

He stated a broader statewide action may 73 ultimately be beneficial to ensure consistency among municipalities and avoid shifting development 74 pressures from one community to another. He noted that he had discussed the issue with state officials 75 and referenced the possibility of state-level permitting actions. Public comments expressed concern that 76 state action may not occur quickly enough and encouraged the Board to consider a local moratorium to 77 provide additional time for research and ordinance development. 78 Ms.

Crystall noted that the economic benefits associated with data centers in New Hampshire may differ 79 from those realized in states such as Virginia, where personal property taxes are assessed on equipment 80 and infrastructure located within such facilities. She stated that evaluating future data center proposals 81 would require consideration of both potential tax revenue and possible impacts on residents, public health, 82 and the long-term character of the community. 83 Ms. Judith Attorri, 9 Currier Drive, also suggested that the matter be presented for broader public input, 84 noting that any future data center development could have significant impacts on the community. 85 Ms.

Makinen presented a draft ordinance framework addressing data centers and other large energy- 86 consuming uses. The draft was modeled after the Town's wireless communications facilities regulations 87 and would establish a conditional use permit process with specific performance standards tailored to 88 large-scale data processing facilities. Vice Chair Crystall also asked whether cryptocurrency mining 89 operations should be incorporated within the definition of regulated facilities. 90 Selectman McDaniel discussed the possibility of holding public hearings on both a proposed moratorium 91 and potential zoning amendments. Mr.

Pietrangelo noted that while a moratorium could be drafted and 92 considered within a relatively short timeframe, comprehensive zoning ordinance amendments would 93 likely require additional research and public review before being finalized. 94 Mr. Pietrangelo discussed the potential duration of a moratorium and the process for enacting a proposed 95 moratorium. Selectman McDaniel advised that a moratorium could remain in effect for up to one year and 96 explained that statutory protections would take effect upon the posting of a public hearing notice and the 97 proposed ordinance language and would be on the ballot like a zoning amendment. Ms.

Makinen noted 98 that, when posting a public hearing notice, the Board must also make the proposed ordinance language 99 available to the public for review and cannot post a hearing notice before the draft document is prepared. 100 The Board reviewed the draft moratorium ordinance and discussed revisions needed to ensure compliance 101 with the requirements of RSA 674:23. Ms. Hayden noted that the draft should more clearly define what 102 constitutes a data center and ensure the definition is broad enough to encompass all applicable large-scale 103 digital processing facilities, including potential cryptocurrency mining operations. Ms.

Makinen also 104 discussed the need to incorporate written findings describing the unusual circumstances supporting a 105 moratorium and to outline a clear course of action and study process consistent with RSA requirements. 106 Mr. Pietrangelo raised responsibility for conducting the required research, the potential use of expert 107 consultants, legal review costs, and the overall scope of the study effort. Ms. Makinen advised that limited 108 consulting assistance could potentially be funded through existing budget resources; however, the extent 109 of any additional professional services required was not yet known.

110 During public comment, Kendra Ford of 350 New Hampshire offered to assist the Town in identifying 111 research organizations, foundations, and other resources studying data center development and its 112 impacts. She noted that substantial research is already being conducted by government and non- 113 government organizations and suggested that existing information may help support the Town's review 114 process. Board members discussed the importance of obtaining objective and balanced information from 115 reliable sources as part of any future study effort. 116 Selectman McDaniel made a motion that was seconded by Ms. Crystall to direct Ms.

Makinen to refine 117 the proposed temporary moratorium ordinance for review in a public hearing at the December 3, 2026 118 Zoning Board Amendment Review meeting. Location to be determined. Located at 116-120 South Bow Road; Map 42, Block 2, Lot 36-B; 22 Zone: Rural (RU) 23 Attorney Brian Grossman of Strang, Scott & Giroux, LLP, Louis Vitali of Mariner Tower, and project engineer 24 Sylvester Bhembe presented updates from the last meeting.

The applicant reported that the third-party stormwater 25 review had been completed and all engineering comments had been resolved to the satisfaction of the Town’s 26 reviewing engineer. 27 Discussion focused on an ephemeral stream crossing discovered during the site review. Board members discussed state 28 permitting requirements, local wetland jurisdiction, and potential conditions of approval requiring all applicable state 29 permits. The Board determined that a Wetland Protection CUP was not required for buffer impacts to the ephemeral 30 stream. 31 The Board also reviewed utility pole placement along the driveway. Mr.

Bhembe confirmed that the edge of driveway 32 does not come within 15 feet of the property line, and the utility poles are all at least 20 feet from the property line. 33 Chair Berube, Jr. opened the public hearing at 7:16 PM. 34 Ms. Makinen read a comment letter submitted by abutter Dana Ordway. Mr. Ordway expressed concerns regarding a 35 previously requested NH Natural Heritage Bureau (NHB) and NHDES Wildlife Screening document that had not been 36 included in the application materials. Ms. Makinen noted that the document had been submitted and that no impacts 37 were identified.

Additional concerns raised in the letter included potential impacts to the ephemeral stream and 38 associated buffers, overhead utility encroachment into buffer areas, setbacks and forest canopy impacts, winter 39 maintenance of the access driveway, the justification for the requested lease area reduction waiver, the adequacy of the 40 proposed $50,000 decommissioning bond, and protections for state and federally endangered species. 41 Susan Moore asked whether the proposed drainage system addressed concerns regarding runoff onto an adjacent 42 downhill property. Mr.

Grossman stated that all stormwater would be retained on-site and acknowledged that the 43 project would result in less runoff leaving the site than currently exists. 44 Chair Berube, Jr. closed the public hearing at 7:20 PM. 45 Ms. Makinen responded that she spoke to André Garron, the Hookset Town Administrator, the morning of October 15, 46 2026, to make sure she had the most up-to-date information on their tower situation. No viable collocation 47 opportunities currently exist, and she provided updated information regarding the Hooksett and State-owned tower 48 sites.

49 The Board discussed the request for a waiver from Site Plan Regulations Section 5.02.J requiring utilities to be placed 50 underground. Mr. Grossman stated that extending underground electric service to the proposed facility would require 51 trenching for approximately one-quarter mile along the access drive, resulting in significant cost and unnecessary 52 disturbance to existing vegetation. Mr. Grossman further explained that the existing vegetative cover would adequately 53 screen the utility line and that utility poles located along the access drive would have minimal visual impact.

The 54 Board discussed potential concerns regarding downed trees and utility interruptions and concluded that the width of the 55 access easement, driveway layout, and pole locations would minimize such concerns. 56 The Board next reviewed a waiver request from Site Plan Regulations Section 5.02.T requiring monumentation of the 57 property. Mr. Grossman noted that the parent parcel contains approximately 57 acres, while the proposed development 58 would disturb less than one percent of the property. Given the size of the parcel and the limited extent of the proposed 59 improvements, Mr. Grossman stated that monumentation was unnecessary and would not provide a practical benefit.

60 The Board found that the waiver was reasonable given the scope of the project and the characteristics of the site. 61 Ms. Makinen noted that when reviewing the next two waiver requests from PWSF Zoning Ordinance provisions, the 62 Board will need to apply the criteria set forth in Article 13.02 B. 2. a. for unnecessary hardship. 63 The Board then reviewed a waiver request from Zoning Ordinance Section 7.10.E.2.b requiring tower camouflage. Mr. 64 Grossman testified that at the proposed height of approximately 190 feet, camouflage measures would be ineffective 65 and would likely make the structure more visually prominent. Mr.

Grossman explained that a standard lattice tower 66 would be less noticeable because of its open design and that attempting to disguise the tower as another feature would 67 draw additional attention to it. The Board discussed the visual impacts of the proposed tower and found that strict 68 compliance with the camouflage requirement would not achieve the intended purpose of minimizing visibility. 69 The final waiver request is from Zoning Ordinance Section 7.10.E.4 requiring site control over an area equal to 125 70 percent of the tower height. Mr.

Grossman explained that compliance with this requirement would require control of 71 approximately four acres, which is substantially larger than the industry-standard lease area of 75 feet by 75 feet to 100 72 feet by 100 feet. Mr. Grossman stated that the larger site control area would create unnecessary costs and place an 73 undue burden on the property owner while limiting future use of a significant portion of the property without providing 74 additional public benefit. Mr. Grossman further noted that the proposed tower meets all required setbacks from 75 property boundaries and that similar waivers have been granted for previously approved wireless communication 76 facilities in Town.

The Board discussed the intent of the ordinance, the size of the subject parcel, and the lack of 77 impact on neighboring properties, and found the requested waiver to be reasonable and consistent with prior approvals. 78 Selectman McDaniel made a motion to approve waivers for Section 5.02.J (underground utilities) and Section 5.02.T 79 (monumentation). The motion was seconded by Ms. Duke and the Board voted unanimously in favor. 80 Selectman McDaniel made a motion to approve waivers for Section 7.10.E(2)(b) regarding tower camouflage and 81 Section 7.10.E(4) regarding site control area requirements. The motion was seconded by Ms. Duke and the Board 82 voted unanimously in favor.

83 Selectman McDaniel made a motion to approve Applications 208-26 and 407-26 subject to the following conditions: 84 1. Obtain all required state permits. 85 2. Execute a tower removal bond in the amount of $50,000 prior to construction. 86 3. Submit proof of appropriate liability insurance with respect to the proposed PWSF prior to construction. 87 4. Agreement with the Town of Bow to allow maximum collocation opportunities. 88 5. Permit inspection by the Board of Selectmen or its designee. 89 6. Obtain a Town driveway permit. 90 7. Record the Notice of Decision at the Merrimack County Registry of Deeds. 93 The motion was seconded by Ms. Duke and the Board voted unanimously in favor. 94 Selectman McDaniel made a motion to approve the following Findings of Fact: 95 1. It is a public good to have ample cell phone coverage, including for safety issues. 96 2. The Board received testimony from both the applicant and abutters over multiple meetings. 97 3. The Board applied the ordinances as they interpret them. 98 4. The Board consulted with a third-party engineer. 99 5. The Board confirmed multiple times that there is no other viable collocation tower in the area. 100 6.

The approved waiver requests satisfy the applicable ordinance criteria. 101 The motion was seconded by Ms. Duke and the Board voted unanimously in favor. 102 3. Application no. 410-26: Daniel and Chelsea Frost 103 After-the-Fact Wetland Protection Conditional Use Permit for approximately 4,500 sq. ft. wetland buffer 104 impacts for a residential driveway and garage. Located at 5 Heidi Lane; Map 20, Block 5, Lot 67-A1; Zone: 105 Residential (R) 106 Ms. Frost explained that they had obtained building permits for garage and driveway improvements and were unaware 107 that a wetland buffer impact had occurred. The issue was discovered during a later inspection for a separate permit.

108 The applicants worked with a wetland scientist to delineate wetlands and proposed mitigation planting to restore 109 disturbed buffer areas. 110 Board members discussed the extent of the buffer impact, wetland delineation, Town permitting processes, and 111 recommendations from the Conservation Commission. Ms. Frost shared photographs of the property with the Board 112 and reviewed their proposed planting plan which includes native species such as blueberry bushes, silky dogwood, and 113 bare root trees. 114 Selectman McDaniel made a motion to accept Application 410-26 as complete. The motion was seconded by Ms. Duke 115 and the Board voted unanimously in favor. 116 Ms.

Crystall discussed a few concerns raised by the Conservation Commission including the lack of a formal plan 117 showing the limits and size of the disturbed area. The Conservation Commission also requested an explanation of how 118 this was able to occur. 119 Ms. Makinen explained that the inspector did not pick up on the nearby wetlands when reviewing the permit in the 120 office. This problem was exacerbated by the fact that no inspections were requested for the garage project. Typically, 121 the inspector would be on site early on in the construction process and would have likely noticed the wetland buffer 122 impacts then.

We are adjusting our process in the office to better assess zoning compliance with building permits 123 before they are issued. 124 Chair Berube, Jr. opened the public hearing at 7:54 PM. 125 Marilyn Lull shared that it’s better to plant trees and shrubs in the fall, because they can take root through the winter 126 and then come back in the spring. Ms. Crystall agreed and said that she can share a list of native species to consider. 127 Gil Rogers of Jonathan Lane agreed with the Board that the Town bears some responsibility for the situation. He noted 128 his understanding was that the owner had approached the Town for advice but did not receive adequate guidance.

He 129 acknowledged that a permit had been obtained for the work; however, the impacts were not properly identified. Mr. 130 Rogers stated that, had the application come before the Board prior to the work being completed, it likely would have 131 faced challenges due to the wetland filling and impacts within the buffer, particularly without a clear mitigation plan. 132 He concluded that the Town should improve its process by providing earlier site review and expert guidance to 133 property owners so they are aware when proposed work may be difficult to permit and obtain approval for. 134 Chair Berube, Jr. closed the public hearing at 7:58 PM.

135 Selectman McDaniel made a motion that Application 410-26 does not have regional impact. The motion was seconded 136 by Ms. Duke and the Board voted unanimously in favor. 137 Selectman McDaniel made a motion to approve Application 410-26 with the following conditions: 138 1. Remove rock and pea gravel from the wetland buffer. 139 2. Install wetland buffer markers at the 50-foot wetland buffer boundary or the most distant location if less than 140 50 feet. 141 3. Implement the planting plan using species on the lists provided by the Town and Conservation Commission. 142 The motion was seconded by Ms. Duke and the Board voted unanimously in favor.

143 Selectman McDaniel made a motion to approve the following Findings of Fact that the approved plan is the most 144 appropriate way to move forward to mitigate damage to the wetland. The motion was seconded by Ms. Duke and 145 approved unanimously. 146 4. Application no. 210-26: 6 Tallwood LLC (Bedford Design Consultants, Inc.) 147 Site Plan Review for a 4-building self-storage facility totaling 14,000 sq. ft. 148 Located at 6 Tallwood Drive; Map 35, Block 2, Lot 190-D; Zone: General Industrial (I-2). 149 George Chadwick of Bedford Design Consultants presented the proposal. The site consists of approximately 4.3 acres 150 in the General Industrial (I-2) Zone.

The proposal includes four self-storage buildings, stormwater controls, 151 landscaping, lighting, and associated infrastructure. The applicant stated that no increase in runoff would occur and 152 that all stormwater would be collected and infiltrated on site. 153 In response to checklist item #5, Mr. Chadwick agreed to update the plans with the current Flood Insurance Rate Map 154 (FIRM) date, provide a written operational narrative describing facility operations, access, and hours of use (checklist 155 #40). Mr.

Coleman provided information identifying the uses and activities that would be permitted at the facility, 156 noting that no hazardous waste or chemicals would be stored or used on-site. The Board determined that a site walk 157 was not necessary as Chair Berube Jr. and Selectman McDaniel had been to the site recently. 158 Mr. Chadwick stated that additional landscaping would be installed along Tallwood Drive to supplement existing 159 vegetation and provide screening from the roadway. Any relocated evergreen trees that do not survive would be 160 replaced with native vegetation. Mr.

Chadwick stated that the development is located within an existing industrial area 161 and is largely screened by vegetation, topography, and surrounding development. The Board agreed that the facility 162 would have limited visibility from the roadway and that the proposed landscaping would provide adequate screening. 163 Mr. Chadwick requested a waiver from Section 5.02.T (Monumentation) (checklist #13) to waive installation of an 164 additional monument along a 552-foot undeveloped property line, citing steep terrain, dense woods, and a lack of 165 development potential in the area. 166 Mr.

Chadwick addressed the comment of lighting at the entrance gate by explaining that gate lighting was not 167 proposed due to concerns about light spillover into the Town right-of-way and noted that automated gate access, 168 vehicle headlights, an illuminated access screen, and existing nearby lighting would provide adequate visibility. The 169 Board agreed that additional gate lighting was not necessary. 170 Mr. Pietrangelo asked if snow storage and snowmelt would negatively affect the infiltration basin or groundwater 171 resources and Mr.

Chadwick explained that the snow storage area is located outside the basin area and agreed to 172 address maintenance measures through the stormwater maintenance plan, make grading adjustments if necessary, and 173 utilize a Green SnowPro-certified snow removal contractor. The Board was satisfied that the proposed snow storage 174 and management practices adequately addressed stormwater and groundwater protection concerns. 175 Selectman McDaniel made a motion to accept Application 210-26 as complete. The motion was seconded by Ms. Duke 176 and carried unanimously. 177 Chair Berube, Jr. opened and closed the public hearing at 8:25 PM.

178 Selectman McDaniel made a motion that Application 210-26 does not have regional impact. The motion was seconded 179 by Mr. Barry and carried unanimously. 180 Selectman McDaniel made a motion to approve a waiver from Section 5.02.T regarding monumentation. The motion 181 was seconded by Ms. Duke and carried unanimously. 182 Selectman McDaniel made a motion to approve Application 210-26 with the following conditions: 183 1. All driveway access shall be at least 15 ft. back from the property line and indicated on the plan as such. 184 2. Address missing checklist items (updated FIRM date) 185 3. Obtain all required state and local permits. 186 4.

Submit final plans with professional stamps and owner signature. 187 5. All conditions of approval and waivers shall appear on the final plan. 188 6. Utilize Green SnowPro-certified operators for snow management. 189 7. Submit an operational brief for the facility. 190 The motion was seconded by Ms. Duke and carried unanimously. 191 Selectman McDaniel made a motion to approve the following Finding of Fact: 192 1. The proposed self-storage facility constitutes appropriate use of the property and is consistent with the Town’s 193 zoning regulations. 194 The motion was seconded by Ms. Duke and carried unanimously.

Trucking on Dow Road Town Manager Stack reported that he received a concern from a resident who lives at the corner of Dow Road and Knox Road. Town Manager Stack consulted Police Chief Miller regarding the issue.

BOW HERITAGE COMMISSION OCTOBER 13TH, 2026 MEETING MINUTES Call to order - 2:00 pm Guests and Volunteers - Connor Parzick, Tom Wilson, Dick & Alna Stevens,Candy Ricard and Kay Herrick. Tom Wilson developed the Barns of Bow website. He is retiring the site and would like the Town of Bow to continue with the site or copy the files. He has a thumbdrive of the site with him.The Town’s policy is to be wary of copied files in case of infected material. Jim states that Tonia transfers the files and then places them on our website. Tom says when he downloads the site he loses the edges and it becomes “larger”.

John then asks Connor about this and Connor replies that the Town could create another page and (copy and paste)upload the pics and text. Connor works for the SAU not the Town. Tom asks if we want to accept the thumbdrive or give it to Connor? Connor could troubleshoot the problem Tom was having. Dave W. moves that the BHC accept the Barns of Bow thumbdrive and give it to Connor.John seconds the motion. No further discussion and the Ayes have it, 7 to 0. Motion passes. It is in Connor’s possession. Connor Parzick asks if we have candidates and a series of questions we usually ask?

We have a brief series of questions asked but some come “off the cuff” depending on the comfort of the interviewee. He asks if we were to purchase the equipment, Connor can then edit (post production) and distribute the finished video via YouTube, etc. Connor can set the controls and configure the camera, back-up battery, memory card,etc. It gets the ability done for a great finished product.Could he check for discounts? Of course. Dik asks if we need the tri-pod? It probably would be good to invest in case Eric’s isn’t available. John asks if Connor can email Eric and loop John in? Email is the best choice to get in touch with Connor. The average time for an interview is one hour.

Connor told us that all the VHS tapes from the BHS have been downloaded to YouTube.Send us the link? We all thank him very much! GENERAL BUSINESS - Attendance - Eric Anderson, Chair; Sue Wheeler,Secretary; Dik Dagavarian, Treasurer; Dave Lindquist, Jim Dimick, John Urdi, and Dave West. Absent are Don Fournier and Eleana Colby, BoS representative. Minutes - Eric did not receive them so we will approve next month. Financials - The OB expended $179.78 in September with a balance remaining of $1820.22. Buying the camera and equipment,office supplies, preservation & restoration comes out of the OB. The HF was somewhat restricted in some money many years ago.

The HF monthly interest is $76.07as of last month and the balance is $25,498.89. Connor Parzick has the list of items for us to purchase for interviewing our citizens. The list contains; camcorder, battery & extras, charger & cord. Memory card and tri-pod. Dave West moves to authorize an expenditure of up to $1500.00 to purchase the video equipment (as Connor suggests) for interviews. Dave L. seconds the motion. No further discussion and the Ayes have it, 7 to 0. Dik makes a motion to reimburse Eric for the purchase of a multi-height exhibit table to hold the voting items in the Heritage room at the price of $44.98. Dave W. seconds the motion. Ayes have it, 7 to 0. Both motions passed.

Correspondence - NH Historical Society newsletter, 5 Barns of Bow posters, and a Preservation Alliance newsletter. ZBA is a no go. OLD BUSINESS - There was none covered at this particular meeting. NEW BUSINESS - Select Board report - John asks if we can ask the Town Manager for more involvement? Eric suggests involving the Chair of the selectman. Andrew Jackson Sign - The State has taken the sign and is reconditioning it. They will re-install it when completed. Cheryl M. asks, when the State re-installs the sign can the BHC celebrate? Some kind of ceremony involving the State representatives or such? Chuck Douglas may let us know.

Other business - Chris Andrews tells us that the CIP will meet tomorrow night. Chris’ budget will include phase # 1 is construction at the BBMH and phase # 2 will be the painting of the building. The OTH will be painted next spring with a few repairs. Windows at the OTH to reglaze was quoted at $24,000.00 last year. This year the quote is $20,00.00 with painting. Chris is looking to get a registry application underway. At the BCSH there is lead paint inside and needs more scraping. (There is no ability to do it in house). OB quote was $12,000.00 possibly starting in July. There is a new phone system underway. So send your emails to Chris. There is no greeting as of now.

It will take a couple of weeks to get the system up and working. Dave W. asks if the new lighting downstairs is LED? And will it eventually wash out photos? Chris will inquire, just email him. He tells us that Unitil paid 90% of the lighting project. It was a one year project event. IMPORTANT DATES - BHC Meetings - Nov. 10th and Dec. 8th at 9 - 11 am, Room C. BHC Scheduled to Brief Select Board at 5pm Oct. 13th, about its 2026 activities. Nov. 3rd, Election Day 7am-7pm at BMS Work Sessions - Tuesdays and Fridays from Oct. 19th til Nov. 6th, 9am til noon. Bow Heritage Commission’s Open House, Saturday November 14th, 10 am til 3 pm. Bow Heritage Day at the BBMH , Saturday Nov.

21st, 11am - 1pm. (Winterizing the building with bell ringing for all) Adjourn - Dave L. moves to adjourn with Dave W. seconding the motion. Ayes have it, 7 to 0 adjourning at 3:40 pm. Respectfully submitted, Sue Wheeler, BHC Secretary

TOWN OF BOW Planning Board 10 Grandview Road, Bow, New Hampshire 03304 Phone (603) 223-3976 | Fax (603) 225-2982 | Website www.bownh.gov 1 Master Plan Steering Committee Minutes October 6, 2026 The Town of Bow Master Plan Steering Committee met on Tuesday, October 6, 2026, at 6:00 PM in Meeting Room C of the Bow Municipal Building, 10 Grandview Road, Bow, NH. Members Present: Tom O’Donovan, John Muras, Sandra Crystall, Jill Hadaway, Melynie Klunk, Nancy Rheinhardt, Kristen Hayden, Addison Hartman. Others Present: Karri Makinen, Town of Bow Community Development Director;

Mike Tardiff, Central NH Regional Planning Commission (CNHRPC) Executive Director, Craig Tufts, CNHRPC Senior GIS/Transportation Planner, Sarah Hewitt, Community and Environmental Planner and Danyelle Gourley, Town of Bow Land Use Assistant. The meeting was called to order at 6:05 PM. Call to Order and Introductions The meeting began with introductions of committee members and attendees. Sarah Hewitt introduced herself and noted that she joined the CNHRPC on July 1. Mr. Tardiff welcomed attendees and stated that the Committee is at an important point in the development of the Land Use Chapter of the Master Plan.

He noted that several ongoing and emerging issues, including potential data center development, redevelopment opportunities at the former Merrimack Station site, the Bow Mills Strategic Plan, and proposed improvements at Interstate 89 Exit 1, should be considered as part of the long-term vision for the community. Potential Data Center Development Mr. Tardiff opened a discussion regarding potential future data center development within the Town. Ms. Makinen clarified that no formal application has been submitted to the Town and that only preliminary study discussions have occurred.

Members discussed the regulatory framework associated with data centers and noted that oversight would involve multiple agencies, including the New Hampshire Department of Environmental Services (NHDES) and the Public Utilities Commission (PUC), in addition to local reviews. Discussion focused on identifying issues that may be appropriately addressed through local regulations versus those handled by state and federal agencies. Committee members questioned how future data center proposals should be addressed within the Master Plan. Discussion focused on whether the Land Use Chapter should reference performance standards for issues such as:

Page 2 of 3 • Noise • Vibration • Energy consumption • Water use • Environmental impacts Mr. Tardiff noted that many municipalities are currently evaluating how best to regulate data centers and that communities across the region are exploring updates to site plan regulations and performance standards. Members agreed that topics such as noise and vibration may warrant additional attention within local regulations and could be highlighted within the Master Plan as areas for future evaluation. Ms. Klunk asked whether past Town boards have historically relied on the Master Plan when making decisions.

Staff responded that the Master Plan serves as a foundational policy document and is often referenced when considering zoning amendments and long-range planning initiatives. Mr. O’Donovan discussed the importance of public education regarding potential data center development and recommended reviewing the Select Board public comment session from September 22, which included extensive discussion regarding community concerns, permitting processes, and regulatory authority. Ms. Klunk expressed concern that technology is advancing rapidly and that the Master Plan should be written in a manner that remains flexible enough to address future emerging land uses and technologies.

Interstate 89 Exit 1 Improvements Mr. Tufts reviewed recent developments regarding proposed transportation improvements near Interstate 89 Exit 1. He reported that discussions with the New Hampshire Department of Transportation (NHDOT) indicate that while funding for the full interchange project remains uncertain, recent adjustments to transportation funding may allow certain safety improvements to move forward earlier than anticipated. He noted that Exit 1 has been identified as a priority location for safety improvements and that repairs to red-listed bridges remain an important component of the overall project.

Committee members reviewed a conceptual plan for the proposed interchange improvements and discussed: • Traffic circulation changes • Access to Route 3-A • Safety improvements • Signalized intersections • Pedestrian and bicycle accommodations • Potential impacts on future development opportunities Ms. Klunk expressed concern regarding the removal of direct southbound access and questioned whether traffic volumes would increase on local roads. Page 3 of 3 Members discussed the possibility of incorporating sidewalks, bicycle facilities, or multi-use paths into future transportation improvements to improve connectivity between schools, the library, Bow Mills, and other community destinations.

There was consensus that additional information from NHDOT would be beneficial. Ms. Makinen discussed inviting NHDOT representatives to a future meeting to provide an overview of the project status and next steps. Members agreed that a presentation from project managers would help the Committee better understand the project and develop Master Plan recommendations. Bow Mills Redevelopment Strategy Ms. Makinen provided an update on the Bow Mills Redevelopment Strategy. She reported that Resilience Planning and Design is currently completing the existing conditions analysis.

She discussed an engagement opportunity that will include a Business After Hours event on November 4 at Merrimack County Savings Bank, where business owners will be invited to discuss their vision and future needs for the Bow Mills area. Discussion focused on the importance of infrastructure planning, including water service, transportation access, and pedestrian connectivity, to support future redevelopment goals. 12 Logging Hill Road Members discussed continued interest in the development at 12 Logging Hill Road property. Ms. Makinen reported that property owners continue to work with NHDOT regarding driveway permits and traffic studies.

A recent project scoping meeting has been completed, and traffic engineering materials have been submitted for review. Committee members discussed possible future uses, including warehousing and distribution facilities, and noted that any proposed development would need to comply with applicable zoning requirements. Several members emphasized the importance of maintaining the community gateway character of the area and ensuring future development is consistent with Town goals. The Committee reviewed the draft minutes from their previous meeting on July 14, 2026. A motion was made by Sandy Crystall and seconded by Kristen Hayden to approve the minutes all were in favor.
The next meeting is scheduled for Monday, November 9 at 6:00 PM. Adjournment Sandy Crystall made a motion to adjourn, Kristen Hayden seconded, and the meeting was adjourned.

1 September 22, 2026 Board of Selectmen Meeting Approved Minutes September 22, 2026 On Tuesday, September 22, 2026, at 6:00 p.m., the Board of Selectmen met in Meeting Room A, at the Bow Municipal Building, 10 Grandview Road, Bow, NH 03304. CALL TO ORDER Chair McDaniel called the meeting to order at 6:00 p.m. Present: Chair Kip McDaniel, Vice Chair Ian Flanagan, Selectwoman Angela Brennan, Selectwoman Eleana Colby, Town Manager David Stack, Executive Assistant Tonia Lindquist, and members of the public. Not present: Selectman Chris Nicolopoulos II.

PUBLIC COMMENT Chair McDaniel welcomed the public, he acknowledged by the number of people present they were here to speak to the recent article in the Concord Monitor about a potential data center in the former powerplant building, in the Town of Bow. Chair McDaniel noted that the data center was not on the agenda, however, anyone wanting to speak about the matter could do during public comment. Before comments were heard, Chair McDaniel went over in detail the process that developers would need to follow in order to bring forth a proposed data center to the planning and zoning boards and that along the way in the process the public would be notified of public hearings, meetings etc.

Chair McDaniel confirmed that the final decision would come from the planning board, not the Board of Selectmen. Public Comments were heard from Bow residents Robert Johnson 75 Bow Center Road, Kris Hancarik 1250 Route 3A, Susan Moore 11 Crockett Drive, Barbara Bennett 3 Tower Hill Drive, Milo Cocola 5 Nesbitt Drive, Lyn Lull 26B Grandview Road, Scott Coulombe 18 Merrill Crossing, and Linda Millman 80 Robinson Road. All but one resident was against having a data center in Bow.

Public comments were also heard from non-residents Claire Edmonds, Nashua, NH, Beth Hamilton- Karas, Pembroke, NH, Al Benbow, New Market, NH, Kendra Ford, Portsmouth, NH in addition to her comments she provided Chair McDaniel with a signed petition for 350.org. Executive Councilor Karen Liot Hill, Lebanon, NH, State Rep. David Luneau, Hopkinton, NH, Lucas Cariaty, Hooksett, NH and Dr. Robert Feder, Hollis, NH who were also not in favor of a data center in Bow. Chair McDaniel noting he may have missed some people made one last request for anyone wishing to speak.

Final comments were heard from Charlie Giamette 3 Ferry Road, Bow, NH, Susan Belair 8 Edgewood Drive, Bow, NH and Katie Vozella, a former resident of Bow, NH who also were not in favor of having a data center in Bow. 2 September 22, 2026 III. PUBLIC HEARINGS - none IV. MEETINGS 1. Bow Pioneers Snowmobile Club – Mark Dube Mark Dube, Trail Master Bow Pioneers Snowmobile Club gave an update on the various bridge work being done by the club on private property with owner permission, and trail maintenance the club has lined up. Mr. Dube also noted there were three changes to the landowner list.

A MOTION was made by Selectwoman Brennan and seconded by Vice Chair Flanagan to approve the use of town land by the Bow Pioneers Snowmobile Club. MOTION PASSED 4-0. Selectwoman Brennan thanked Mr. Dube for a great report and noted the improvements the club is making. V. CONSENT AGENDA 1. Appointment 300th Celebration Committee – Greg Cordier 2. Appointment Drinking Water Protection Committee – Ryan Berg 3. Utility Billing Warrant - Water A MOTION was made by Selectwoman Colby and duly seconded by Selectwoman Brennan to approve the consent agenda as presented. MOTION PASSED 4-0. VI. TOWN MANAGER’S REPORT Administration Employee of the Month:

The employee of the month for September is Emily Dorman from the Town Facilities Department. Congratulations, Emily! NHMA Legislative Policy Conference: I attended the conference last week and served as the Town’s representative. I will forward a copy of the conference report. Facilities New phone system: Fidium has delayed the installation of the system until October 13. Fire Grants: The Department has been awarded a $25,000 federal grant for the purchase of a ventilator. I had previously reported that an application had been submitted. Public Works Household Hazardous Waste Collection Day: I recently signed a contract with NH Recycles to conduct the collection.

The event will be held on Saturday, October 17 at the DPW facility. Selectwoman Colby reminded the public and those in attendance that this year you will need to provide proof of residency for Bow or Dunbarton. 3 September 22, 2026 Town Manager Stack also reported that the state paving project will commence on September 27, 2026. Mike Hague Foreman with the Public Works Department will be retiring in October. Vice Chair Flanagan asked about the ambulance and was the town down to just one? Town Manager Stack reported the second ambulance has been sent off for repairs and it is due to be replaced in a couple of years. VII. DISCUSSION/ACTION ITEMS 1.

Acceptance of August 11, 2026, Meeting Minutes A MOTION was made by Vice Chair Flanagan and seconded by Selectwoman Colby to approve the August 11, 2026, meeting minutes as amended. Follow up:

Have the department heads and budget committee attend the December 1, 2026, meeting and share the budget meeting schedule with the budget committee. 3. Perambulation Bow/Dunbarton Chair McDaniel summarized a letter the board received from Line Comeau, Town Administrator of Dunbarton requesting to schedule a perambulation site walk between Bow and Dunbarton which is required every 7 years. Town Manager Stack informed the Board that usually a member of the board will participate in the perambulation site walk. Chair McDaniel volunteered to participate in the site walk.

A MOTION was made by Selectwoman Brennan and seconded by Selectwoman Colby to nominate Chair McDaniel to join the Town of Dunbarton for the Bow/Dunbarton Perambulation site walk. MOTION PASSED 4-0. 4. Audible Crossing Update Town Manager Stack reported that the cost to install an audible crosswalk would be between $22,000 to $23,000. In talking with DPW Director Sweeney to have an audible sidewalk located between Bow Middle School and Bow Recreation Center would be difficult in that location because the current 4 September 22, 2026 sidewalk now does not meet ADA requirements, and to install a new one would require switchbacks because of the slope up to the parking lot. Follow up:

The Board would like Town Manager Stack to reach out to the school for their input. VIII. REPORTS 1. Board Committee Reports Selectwoman Brennan updated the Board on the CIP Committee and Selectwoman Colby gave an update on the 300th Celebration Committee. IX. BOTTOM LINES Chair McDaniel: reported he received a wonderful note from the Chair of the School Board about the recent incident at the high school on how well our police department coordinated to help investigate and bring a resolution to that problem and it was nice to receive a note from Martin saying how proud he was with the police department, so thank you to them. Selectman Nicolopoulos: not present Selectwoman Brennan:

I want to thank everyone who came out today, I want to echo your earlier remarks Chair McDaniel, everyone was very respectful in their comments to the board, and just a reminder this board is not in control of a data center, we have not seen anything, we do not have any information and it is not this board’s responsibility. I am thankful that everyone was able to be respectful and I was glad to hear everyone’s comments. Selectwoman Colby:

I just want to thank everyone for a wonderful primary election, it went smooth as usual downright impressive when the middle school kids got out the principal and vice principal had everyone going where they needed to go, and they got kids safely into cars while voters were moving. It went remarkably well. Thank you to everyone at elections and everyone at the Memorial School. Vice Chair Flanagan: I would agree, the elections went very well, and it was very well coordinated. It was inconvenient for pick-ups and drop offs a little bit, but it was just a blip. Everyone did a great job, and we will learn from that. Saturday is Bactoberfest with fireworks, and a 5K. X.

BOW HERITAGE COMMISSION SEPTEMBER 15, 2026 MEETING MINUTES Call to order - 9 am Guests & Volunteers - Candy Ricard and Kay Herrick. GENERAL BUSINESS - Attendance - Eric Anderson, Chair; Sue Wheeler, Secretary; Dik Dagavarian, Treasurer; Jim Dimick, John Urdi, Don Fournier, Dave West, and Dave Lindquist. Absent is Eleana Colby, Board of Selectman representative. Minutes - August 11th minutes were reviewed and discussed. Jim moves to accept the minutes with John seconding the motion. Ayes have it with a vote of 7 to 1 abstention. Motion passes. Financials - The OB has an amount of $2000.00.

With expenditures of a membership renewal from the Preservation Alliance for $50.00 and a total of $93.25 from additional expenses there is a new total of the OB. With $143.25 subtracted, the new total is $1856.75 The HF has received $72.80 in monthly interest with a new total of $23,473.95 in the Heritage Fund. There were no out of pocket expenses this month.Don makes a motion to accept the Treasurer’s report and Dave W.seconds the motion. No further discussion needed. The Ayes have it, 8 to 0. Motion passes. Correspondence - There is a thank you card from the PA for our renewal of membership. ZBA/Planning board has an application received to reconstruct a new sign Dave W.

asks if it is digital? We don’t believe it is. OLD BUSINESS - NH State Register of Historic Places - No news.Still will pursue. National Register of Historic Places - Dave W. narrowed it down from 44 people to assist, to 6 that are here in NH. After researching several people, the name of Kay Holmes stood out with a lot of information and interest on her resume. We hope to learn how to begin and gain some information. And if there are any expenses. Articles released for publication and those in the works - The Bow Times article is out to be delivered soon. We are grateful the Bow Times is giving us a great deal of space w/o cost.

Sycamore Tree Site maintenance - Eric talked to Tim Sweeney about if the DPW could maintain the clearing of the Sycamore tree. There just isn’t enough manpower there at DPW to take on this task. Bill Emerson would like a chunk of the partial fallen maple tree. Dave L has handled an excellent clean-up humbly. Many thanks to Dave and his helpers for taking on this endeavor. He says it may take 3- 4 times annually to keep it clear. We are lucky to have you, Dave. Bow Rotarians - They have banned together to clean up the weeds at the OTH. It looks great. John Urdi says the Garden Club planted the plants and he believes the Rotarians may be the ones to maintain the area.

The Hay rake at the Hammond Preserve is now filled with weeds. It is hard to find anyone to maintain the area. Bow’s Heritage Day - We are realizing that we should concentrate on the Open House November 14th for the Bow Heritage Room. Dave W. suggests “buttoning up “ the BBMH as a “here, come see what we do for winter?” I think I heard Dik mention hot cider, cocoa and possibly donuts to add to the fun. Come Ring the Bell!! This idea is great. Dave W. moves to install the window coverings at BBMH with an invite to the public. Dave L. seconds the motion with the date being Nov. 21st from 11 - 1pm. Kay suggests advertising with the Bow Times October and November. Ayes have it, 8 to 0.

Motion passes. Wilson’s “Barns of Bow” website location - The Town is working on that to download on our page. Heritage Room Exhibit Status - Some photos need to be identified. Several articles could be displayed. Areas need to be cleaned. Books need to be put away that don’t pertain to the town of Bow. It would be nice to put out a guest book and a donation jar. Where is the Foot Warmer? At the BBMH? NEW BUSINESS - Select Board Report - Tabled. EC is absent. Town’s 300th Anniversary - Next meeting is September 21st, at Room C in the municipal building. BHC’s access to the Dam Site on 3A across from Dunckle Rd.- The new building inspector will check into the Mill Site on 3A.

The agreement was to have access to the Mill site. There was supposed to be a driveway and public picnic tables within the former sidewalk. Conditions were to be handled by the Conservation Commission. The notice of decision was in September of 2025. Not sure of the Planning Board’s last decision. Bow’s 100 Oldest Homes - John Urdi made contact with 8 different people to photograph. Nancy Knapp’s house seems to be the oldest. The date is 1719. We need to find the post office sign from that home. Mary Wuellenwebber’s house was an old tavern ( according to Mary) and looks like a museum. John visited Woodhill road #63 and #64 which are photographed as old Colby homesteads.

Also on Woodhill is the old Cheney place. On Hop Kiln road which was an old Brown place they are in the process of rebuilding. At the old Kirchoff place on Brown Hill road, he found no one at home. On Dunbarton Center road, the old Jenks place is currently for sale and no one was there. Names and addresses really help. Recent Submissions to the BHC - There were some more donations from Dick and Alna Stevens. The Andrew Jackson presidential, historical roadside marker- Chuck Douglas would like to find the sign and purchase it. Look for the latest article in the Bow Times about the sign from Cheryl M.

John Urdi’s list of suggested items - John Urdi has had a very difficult time getting in touch with Connor at BHS. We can still do interviews with video and audio. John suggests interviewing Dana Abbott. He is not doing too well as of late. Dave L. list of suggested items - Do we want a sign at the sycamore tree? There is not a good place to park and it is hard to view w/o parking. Jim suggests “Historic Sycamore Tree” with a red arrow? Who makes the signs? What is our plan for the 300th? Dave L. asks can we do signs? One sign should be the same design for all. Eric said he will check with Berube who has made wraps for signs in the past for us. Important Dates - BHC Meetings - Oct.13th, Nov.

10th, and Dec.8th at 9-11 am at Room C. BHC to Brief the Bos at 5pm on Oct. 13 on 2026’s activities. Bow Community Men’s Club - Annual Lobsterfest on Oct.3rd at the community building. Contact Dik for more information. Tickets are also online. Work Sessions - Tuesdays and Fridays from 9am until Noon. BHC “ Bow Heritage Room” OPEN HOUSE , Saturday November 14th from 10am until 3pm. BHC “Winter buttoning up the BBMH” with the public invited November 21st, from 11am until 1pm. Bell ringing is encouraged! BURNING ISSUES - John would like to thank Cheryl for her donation to join the NH Historical Society membership. Jim thinks Eric needs a hard drive for his photos. Did he overwhelm his system?

He suggests using external hard drives so NOT to overwhelm the files. Don asks if the State has proper signage? We think the answer is Yes. Dik has brought zucchini breads galore! One for everybody. Thank you, Dik!! Eric subscribes to two softwares. Publisher and Microsoft Office. Microsoft will be unable to access…. Jim suggests Eric talk to someone at Staples. He also ran across the Facebook post called Granite Whispers. There was a 3minute or so snippet of how Bow NH came to be. It is very well done but done anonymously. ADJOURNMENT - John moves and Dik seconds the motion to adjourn. The Ayes have it, 8 to 0 to adjourn at 11:30 am. Motion passes.
Respectfully submitted, Sue Wheeler, BHC Secretary

CIP Committee –Approved Minutes Page | 1 September 14, 2026 Town of Bow Capital Improvement Committee September 14, 2026 Approved Minutes The Capital Improvement Program (CIP) Committee met, Monday, September 14, 2026 at 5:30 PM in Room B at the Municipal Building, 10 Grandview Road, Bow, NH. Committee members present: Vice Chair Glenn Dugas (Citizen Representative), Harry Judd (Citizen Representative), Martin Osterloh (School Board Representative), Angela Brennan (Selectboard Representative), Jonathan Pietrangelo (Planning Board Representative), and Jeffrey Knight (Budget Committee Representative). Absent (excused): Mark Davis (Citizen Representative). I.

Call to Order The Vice Chair called the meeting to order at 5:30 PM. It was noted that Mark Davis has had to step down from the committee. The Committee then decided to elect a new Chair and Vice Chair. Harry Judd moved to nominate Glenn Dugas for Chair and Jonathan Pietrangelo as Vice Chair. Martin Osterloh seconded. Since there was no further discussion, the vote was called. Motion carried by unanimous vote. II. Approval of Minutes – Harry Judd moved to approve the Committee minutes of August 31, 2026. Glenn Dugas seconded. The Chair called for comment. A typing error was pointed out. Sensing no further comment, the Chair called for a vote.

Minutes of August 31, 2026 approved with a typo correction. Vote: 4-0-1. Martin Osterloh abstained. III. Department Reviews Administration – Property Revaluation CRF – Jeff Knight moved to change the contribution from $20,000 to $17,500 starting with 2027-2028 through 2038-2039. Harry Judd seconded. Motion carried by unanimous vote of the Committee. Bridges and Highway – Annual Paving. The Committee recommended using an inflation rate after 2027-2028 or use a yearly contribution amount of $600,000 through 2038-2039. Bow Bog Culvert ($800,000) was approved at town meeting but has not been drawn down.

The Committee recommends either drawing the Estimated Capital Reserve balance of $38,149 or deducting the same amount from the proposed $150,000 contribution, making the 2027-2028 contribution $121,683. Community Center – The Committee recommended $500,000 as the yearly contribution and will check with the Recreation Director to see if she will be contributing an additional $150,000 for 2027- 2028. Fire Equipment – After some discussion, the Committee recommended changing the yearly contribution from $50,000 to $70,000 to avoid having the fund go into the negative in 2031-2032.

Fire Department – The Committee recommended changing the yearly contribution to the CRF from $300,000 to $290,000 starting in 2027-2028 for five years through 2032-2033. Police – The Committee agreed to have the Police CRF contribution stay at $78,000 as shown in the spreadsheet dated 9/04/2026. The CRF goes into the negative in about 8 years but it will be reviewed again next year. CIP Committee –Approved Minutes Page | 2 September 14, 2026 Public Works – The Committee asked the for updated costs for the Utility Service Truck, Pick-up Truck - Groundskeeper, and Pick-up Truck – Foreman. They also asked how often the Grapple Trailer is used.

Call to Order The Vice Chair called the meeting to order at 5:30 PM. It was noted that Mark Davis has had to step down from the committee. Department Reviews Administration – Property Revaluation CRF – Jeff Knight moved to change the contribution from $20,000 to $17,500 starting with 2027-2028 through 2038-2039. Harry Judd seconded. The Committee recommended using an inflation rate after 2027-2028 or use a yearly contribution amount of $600,000 through 2038-2039. Bow Bog Culvert ($800,000) was approved at town meeting but has not been drawn down.

The Committee recommends either drawing the Estimated Capital Reserve balance of $38,149 or deducting the same amount from the proposed $150,000 contribution, making the 2027-2028 contribution $121,683. Community Center – The Committee recommended $500,000 as the yearly contribution and will check with the Recreation Director to see if she will be contributing an additional $150,000 for 2027- 2028. Fire Equipment – After some discussion, the Committee recommended changing the yearly contribution from $50,000 to $70,000 to avoid having the fund go into the negative in 2031-2032.

Fire Department – The Committee recommended changing the yearly contribution to the CRF from $300,000 to $290,000 starting in 2027-2028 for five years through 2032-2033. Police – The Committee agreed to have the Police CRF contribution stay at $78,000 as shown in the spreadsheet dated 9/04/2026. The CRF goes into the negative in about 8 years but it will be reviewed again next year. TOWN OF BOW Drinking Water Protection Committee 10 Grandview Road, Bow, New Hampshire 03304 (603) 223-3970 | bowdrinkingwater@bownh.gov | www.bownh.gov Location: 10 Grandview Road, Bow Time 5:00 PM UNAPPROVED MINUTES Wednesday, September 9, 2026 Attendees: Cindy Klevens (Chair), Tom O’Donovan, Ken Conaty, Greg Colby, new member Ryan Berg, and Selectboard representative Eleana Colby. Ms. Klevens called the meeting to order at 5 PM. 1. MEETING MINUTES Mr. Conaty moved to approve the June 10, 2026 meeting minutes, seconded by Mr Colby. Approved 4:0. 2. NEW BUSINESS - Northern Borders Grant update – Selectwoman Colby will request and share with the committee.

- Bow Hooksett Watermain Extension Funding Award – the project pre-application for $4 million from the 2026 NHDES Drinking Water State Revolving Loan Fund (DWSRF) was selected for funding. Next steps are to develop a warrant article for approval at Town Meeting Spring 2027, to submit the full funding application documents to NHDES by May 1, 2027, and to begin negotiations with Hooksett Village Water Precinct on the details for an intermunicipal agreement.

- Hooksett Village Water Precinct letter dated 8/31/2026 (attachment 1) – the committee discussed the letter and will develop recommendations for review by the Selectboard as the project is developed further, and once a Water Rate Study can be completed for the Bow Municipal system. Requests include: - Initial supply of 200,000 gpd, reduced from prior request of 600,000 gpd, - Billing at $3.19/1000 gal based on similar wholesale cost from Manchester Water Works supply, - Water quality to meet drinking water standards including new PFOA / PFOS limits of 4 ppt, and - Waiver of connection fees and future capacity development fees. , 4.

OLD BUSINESS - Water Rate Study and DWGTF Consolidation Grant Application – Mr. Berg and Ms. Klevens will develop a scope of work for the Town to obtain quotes from qualified consultants. - Concord City Council status on water main extension to Bow Junction - Selectwoman Colby is coordinating a meeting between Bow representatives and the City Manager.

- Low Salt Corridor Rte 3A / NHDOT Response dated July 2, 2026 (attachment 2) – NHDOT responded favorably to the Town of Bow’s letter dated May 26, 2026, by recommending that the Town obtain the commitment and signatures from Bow DPW, Emergency Response and School Officials and submit a formal letter to the NHDOT Commissioner, to “establish a Type 4 Low Salt Highway in the 1-mile section of Rte 3A located in the municipal wellhead protection area”. Once received, NHDOT can initiate meetings with town officials to develop a Memorandum of Understanding similar to that developed with the Merrimack Water Department. 4.

REGULAR TOPICS Bowdrinkingwater@bownh.gov inquiries – SAU67 School District is hosting a Community Expo on Sept 25, 2026 as part of Homecoming Weekend. The committee will reserve a table to promote private well testing and careers in drinking water. Bow Municipal Water Operations Meeting – Mr Conaty will attend the September meeting. Next meeting is Wednesday, Oct 14, 2025 at 5 PM.
