Town of Bow Buildings & Facilities Advisory Committee Meeting DRAFT June 2, 2026 Present: Chris Andrews (Building and Facilities Manager), David Cook (Chair), Thomas Betteridge (Vice Chair & Secretary), and Glenn Dugas. 1. Call to order. a. David Cook (Chair) Called meeting to order at 6:00 pm. 2. Public Comment a. None 3. Acceptance of the minutes a. Motion to approve the 5/19/2026 meeting minutes by Glenn Dugas, second by David Cook. Unanimous approval. 4. New business: a. CIP Review • Municipal building paving: The paving now includes a few different items more than just paving. The additional items focus on improving parking and building access.

The committee is currently thinking the cost is between $300,000 and 400,000 for all the work. This cost is greater than the $107,200 that was originally in the CIP plan. The committee needs to work which Chris Andrews to develop an estimate of the cost of the work. • Municipal building projects: Siding, windows and insulation addition and replacement projects. Chris is receiving a number for the current project cost to plug into the CIP plan. Concord Conservation Commission – visit The Bow Conservation Commission welcomed Kris Tardiff and Jeff Lewis from the Concord Conservation Commission and Kearsten O’Brien, Sr. Planner for the City of Concord, who attended as part of an effort to strengthen communication and collaboration among neighboring communities. The Bow and Concord Conservation Commissions shared conservation challenges and opportunities that extend across municipal boundaries, emphasizing the importance of regional coordination since natural resources and watersheds do not follow town lines.

Areas such as Turee Pond and the Turkey River watershed were identified as conservation priorities because of their broader environmental benefits. Trail connectivity was a major topic, with Concord noting that public surveys found over 40% of respondents regularly use trails outside city limits, reinforcing the regional nature of recreation. Potential future trail connections, including links to the West End Farm trail system, were discussed along with existing informal use through snowmobile corridors.

Also reviewed were broader conservation land issues, including balancing recreation with wildlife protection, trail impacts, off-trail use, neighboring landowner concerns, and habitat disturbance. Wetland regulations and buffer requirements were compared with discussion focusing on Bow’s varying standards and Concord’s fixed 50-foot buffer approach. Chair Crystall emphasized that wetland functions and ecological value may be unrelated to wetland size. Additional topics included wetland functional assessments, groundwater and aquifer protection, regional GIS mapping improvements, and the importance of distinguishing permanently protected lands from other open space areas.

Conservation focus areas were discussed as useful tools for guiding land acquisition, grant applications, and long-term planning. Funding mechanisms, including land use change tax revenues, conservation bonds, and conservation fund earnings, were reviewed, along with concerns about long-term funding sustainability. The Concord Conservation Commission members discussed its master plan, open space plan, and trail plan in supporting conservation priorities. Trail management generated significant discussion, particularly the need to balance increasing recreational demand with habitat protection.

Commission members also discussed unauthorized Conservation Commission Approved Minutes 05/18/2026 4 trail construction, mountain biking stewardship partnerships, utility corridor impacts, and concerns over wetland disturbances related to Eversource work. Finally, Commission members reviewed challenges associated with online mapping platforms and unofficial trail information (such as the renaming of the Robertson Trail on some apps), emphasizing the ongoing need for monitoring recreation impacts while protecting sensitive conservation resources. Chair Crystall thanked the Concord Conservation Commission for reaching out.

TOWN OF BOW TRUSTEE OF TRUST FUNDS MINUTES May 12, 2026 APPROVED Jon Marvin called the meeting to order at 8:40 AM. Present: Trustees Jon Marvin, Mary Beth Walz and Kate Young, Cambridge Trust Company Representatives Lisa Tourangeau and Brian Bickford Minutes: Review and approval of the January 29, 2026 minutes. New Business: Mr. Bickford provided an overview of the investment markets. Equity markets experienced a pullback in March as a result of the war with Iran but have since recovered. The S & P was down around 7% at the end of March but now is up 8% YTD as first quarter earnings greatly exceeded expectations.

The labor market report last week was better than expected but the latest inflation report was worse than expected so the near term likelihood of the Fed lowering interest rates is pretty much nil. That being said the yield curve is normal and fixed income yields are still attractive and better than average. Corporate profits continue to grow and contrary to what usually happens earnings expectations may actually increase as the year goes on.

As was noted in previous meetings there is some concern about market concentration as the top 10 S & P companies by market capitalization are now close to 40% of the overall S & P whereas in 2015 the top 10 companies made up less than 20% of the overall capitalization. Lastly while gas prices have certainly increased the U.S. economy is less exposed to energy shocks than in prior decades like the 1980’s and 90’s. The Capital Reserve account allocation was 84% fixed income and 16% cash as 4/30/26 so very similar to the allocation at the end of 2025. The total return for the past year was 3.46% which meets the benchmark of 3.48%.

As noted in previous meetings it is tough to beat the benchmark as the benchmark allows for lower fixed income credit risk (down to BBB) then Investment Policy Statement allowed so the Trustees voted at the last meeting to revise the credit ratings limits to allow for investments with ratings of A- or A3. This change will allow for a broadening of investment options. The signed revised IPS was sent to Cambridge who sent a copy to the State of NH. The average credit quality (AA) of the Capital Reserve portfolio remains better than the benchmark.

The current Yield to Maturity (YTM) is 4%, up from 3.7% at our January meeting and the average duration for Capital Reserve funds is 2.12 years (basically the same as last December). Fixed income with a market value of a around $1.2 million matures in 2026 with the majority having very low coupon rates so will arguably be able to re-invest and get better coupon rates. 71% of the account allocation is in government fixed income. The Trust Fund account was up 11.28% YTD as of 4/30 so the performance remains generally better than the benchmarks. The current allocation is 32% in equities with 80% of that allocation invested in domestic equity funds and 20% in international. As usual Mr.

Bickford asked if the town anticipated any income needs in the near future so Mr. Marvin said he would reach out to the Town Finance Director. Lastly there was a discussion regarding the various scholarship funds in the Trust accounts since there have been no distributions for year so Mr. Marvin said he would reach to staff at Bow High School. There being no further business to bring before the Board, the meeting was adjourned at 9:40 AM.

1 May 5, 2026 Board of Selectmen Meeting Approved Minutes May 5, 2026 On Tuesday, May 5, 2026, at 6:00 p.m., the Board of Selectmen met in Meeting Room A, at the Bow Municipal Building, 10 Grandview Road, Bow, NH 03304. This meeting was also live streamed on YouTube https://www.youtube.com/live/Sm-gWuouo-w?si=YkHcVCkMO1jB4__8 I. CALL TO ORDER Chair McDaniel called the meeting to order at 6:00 p.m. Present: Chair Kip McDaniel, Vice Chair Ian Flanagan, Selectwoman Eleana Colby, Town Manager David Stack, Executive Assistant Tonia Lindquist, and members of the public. Not Present: Selectman Chris Nicolopoulos II. PUBLIC COMMENT - None III. PUBLIC HEARING 1.

NH RSA 79-D, Discretionary Preservation Easement application from Timothy and Ashley Polson, 68 Woodhill Road, Tax Map 22-3-4-A. Chair McDaniel opened the public hearing at 6:01 p.m. and provided a brief overview of the application, which included a large barn, a workshop, and a connecting structure between the barn and the main house. A site walk was conducted before the meeting. Chair McDaniel recommended excluding the connecting structure, consistent with the assessor’s recommendation. Hearing no comments from the public, Chair McDaniel closed the public hearing at 6:02 p.m.

A MOTION was made by Selectwoman Colby and seconded by Vice Chair Flanagan to approve the large barn and workshop at 25% and remove the connection building to be taxed at value. MOTION PASSED 4-0. 2. Solar PILOT Lease Entering into Payment in Lieu of Tax Agreement with Kearsarge Bow Schools, LLC Chair McDaniel opened the public hearing at 6:04 p.m. and provided a brief overview of the Payment in Lieu of Tax Agreement for a renewable solar electric generating facility to be built on the Memorial School building. Hearing no public comment, Chair McDaniel closed the hearing at 6:04 p.m.

A MOTION was made Selectwoman Brennan and seconded by Vice Chair Colby to approve the Solar PILOT Lease Entering into payment in Lieu of Tax Agreement with Kearsarge Bow Schools and to authorize Town Manager Stack to sign the necessary documents. MOTION PASSED 4-0. 2 May 5, 2026 IV. MEETINGS 1. Department Update - Fire Chief Dennis Comeau Fire Chief Dennis Comeau provided a department update. He commended his staff and reported that the department is in good shape and fully staffed. The department has responded to 323 calls for service so far this year, and the new forestry truck is nearly complete and should be ready sometime next week. 2.

Quarterly Financial Report – Finance Director Cheryl Lindner Finance Director Cheryl Lindner came before the Board to present the Quarterly Financial Report. She noted revenues are above what is expected, recycling has increased, and property tax collection continues to go well. The Department is preparing for the first half property taxes. V. CONSENT AGENDA 1. Gravel Tax Levy – Jareka Properties LLC – 93.24 2. Intent to Excavate – Route 3A- Ryan Audley 3. Intent to Excavate – Jeff Knight – Gordon Road 4. Intent to Excavate – Katherine Garfield – Gordon Road 5. Intent to Excavate – Katherine Garfield 6.

Utility Billing Warrant – Water A MOTION was made by Selectwoman Brennan and seconded by Selectwoman Colby to approve the consent agenda as presented. MOTION PASSED 4-0. VI. TOWN MANAGER’S REPORT Town Manager Stack reported the following: . Recreation Center Addition: The contract has been signed, and work is scheduled to begin on May 4. LED Lighting upgrades: Contracts have been signed for the Municipal Building and Recreation Center. The order of installation is Recreation Center, Library, Municipal Building. Unitil is funding 90% of the project cost. New phone system: The full install is scheduled for early June.

Facilities Manager Chris Andrews has worked with department heads to determine how programming can or should be updated. A phone inventory has been updated, including an updated database of all employees and e-mail and call preferences for programming. Community Building heat system: The manager has been working with a member of the Facilities Advisory Committee, who has a mechanical engineering background, to develop and RFP and conduct the bid process. 3 May 5, 2026 DPW Ventilation System: The first phase has been completed. It consists of new ventilation system and controls that will automatically activate in the case of elevated harmful gases and supply fresh air.

There are still a few loose ends to close the project out, but the system is fully functional. Bow Mills Study: Karri Makinen and the CNHRPC have finalized an RFP seeking proposals from consultants to develop a Bow Mills Redevelopment Strategy in compliance with the Northern Border Regional Commission (NBRC) Catalyst Grant program. The RFP will be advertised, and I will be managing the project. Dow Road/Route 3A Intersection Project: The Town Attorney is currently reviewing a draft development agreement between the Town and Amber Bow that was submitted by the developer.

The purpose of this agreement is to document the roles and responsibilities of the parties relative to the construction project. The developer will be responsible for contracting for the performance of the work with project oversight by the Town engineer. Once the draft has been reviewed, it will be presented to the Board for discussion and approval. 2026 Tax Liens: Tax liens were executed on 32 properties for 2024 unpaid property taxes. The liens total $203,136.45. VII. The Board reviewed a request from Ridgewood neighbors to hold their third annual neighborhood block party on May 23, 2026. The request included closing Knox Road to Poor Richards Road and was reviewed by the Police Department, Fire Department, and DPW. & TIF Funding for Dow Road/Route 3A Intersection Improvements Selectwoman Colby and Selectwoman Brennan were opposed due to the lack of information in order to make an informed decision and they both wanted the minutes to reflect that. MOTION PASSED 4-0 2. A MOTION was made by Selectwoman Brennan and seconded by Selectwoman Colby to approve the Group Net Meeting Agreement with Kearsarge Bow LF LCC and authorizing Town Manager Stack to sign the necessary documents. 3. Request for Street Closure – Chapter 154-3 Streets and Sidewalks This was addressed earlier in the meeting. 4. Stack Drive Parking The Board discussed the no parking signs on Stack Drive, now that the snow has melted the Board needs to decide on whether to have permanent parking signs.

A MOTION was made by Selectwoman Brennan and seconded by Selectwoman Colby to approve the no parking signs (four of them) to read “no parking from here to corner” on both sides of the road on both sides of the corner that are aesthetically pleasing. TOWN OF BOW Conservation Commission 10 Grandview Road, Bow, New Hampshire 03304 Phone (603) 223-3970 Fax (603) 225-2982 Website: www.bownh.gov Email: conservation@bownh.gov Conservation Commission Approved Minutes Monday, April 13, 2026 The regular meeting of the Bow Conservation Commission was held on Monday, April 13, 2026 at 7:00 PM in Room C of the Municipal Office building at 10 Grandview Road. Chair Sandy Crystall called the meeting to order at 7:02 PM. Commissioners present: Sandy Crystall, Lisa Lindquist, Mary Farrell, Tom O’Donovan, and Dik Dagavarian Other attendees: Ginger Iverson, Recording Secretary 1.

River Road Bridge at Bow Bog Brook – Town Wetland Permit Application The Commission first discussed the River Road bridge over Bow Bog Brook project. This bridge is near where Ferry Road splits off of River Road. The Town has received a permit application prepared by Dubois & King, though it has not yet been formally presented to the Commission. The proposed design includes a 28-foot span bridge, which represents a significant increase over the existing 15-foot corrugated metal pipe arch. While the new design improves hydraulic capacity and stream compatibility, it does not fully meet NHDES stream crossing guidelines requiring a span of 1.2 times the bankfull width.

Commissioners noted that site constraints may limit compliance but agreed to raise questions with the NH Department of Environmental Services (NHDES), including clarification on whether the project lies within a wellhead protection or aquifer area. The Commission plans to submit comments once the application is confirmed with NHDES. Chair Crystall noted that she may adjust the agenda order this evening. 6. Other Planning Board Project Reviews – Loraco Plaza -1494 Route 3-A – Wetland CUP The Commission heard a presentation from Jason Hill of TF Moran and property owner Scott Soucy regarding a proposed commercial development along Route 3-A.

The project entails the construction of two light industrial/flex buildings totaling approximately 8,400 and 3,990 square feet, respectively, with associated parking, drainage, and septic systems. A stormwater management system, previously approved, will be implemented using a bioretention (biofiltration) pond with an underdrain due to high groundwater conditions. The design includes a discharge pipe and level spreader within the wetland buffer, resulting in temporary and permanent impacts. Commissioners asked about buffer impacts, alternative design options, and the length and placement of the drainage pipe.

The applicant explained that site topography, soil conditions, and regulatory setbacks dictated the design. No direct wetland impacts are proposed, and rare species reviews found no concerns. Landscaping plans include mostly native species, though the Commission recommended replacing non-native plantings. Chair Crystall noted that Spiraea Conservation Commission Approved Minutes 04/13/2026 2 japonica is non-native. The Commission expects to participate in a site walk with the Planning Board before making a recommendation. 2.

Project Reviews Robertson Trail – Seasonal reroute – Permit application update, construction schedule The Commission held a site walk earlier in the day at 4 pm in Knox Forest to review the proposed route and revise as needed. Updates included minor route adjustments, construction details, and materials. The boardwalk/puncheon design will likely use larger lumber (3”x 10”s instead of 2”x 10”s) for durability, with no more than one-inch spacing between planks. The total project cost is expected to remain below the budget. Mr.

O'Donovan emphasized the need to finalize construction diagrams for the DES permit application and aim to submit the application by the end of April to allow for late summer construction. Removal of hazardous dead trees along the trail was also supported. Hammond Nature Preserve – Review of current Conservation Restrictions The Commission then revisited the status of the Hammond Nature Preserve and the legal protections governing the land. Mr. O’Donovan noted that Bow Open Spaces believes this property is not effectively protected. A discussion focused on whether the existing conservation restriction provides the same level of protection as a conservation easement.

The Town attorney’s preliminary feedback suggested easements are generally more comprehensive and legally established. The Commissioners agreed to request a legal opinion on whether the current restriction could be altered or removed by Town action. Survey Boundary Markers on Knox Forest (at Knox Road) There was a brief discussion about verifying boundary markers at Knox Forest and confirming whether bounds are present. Chair Crystall will visit the site to confirm the status of the markers. Master Plan – Conservation Lands Review Ms. Crystall shared the schedule for the upcoming Master Plan subcommittee meeting scheduled for April 23, 2026.

Attendance at the visioning session was noted to be low, particularly for the natural resources sessions. Work related to Town conservation land records is ongoing, including deed research to confirm easements or other restrictions. The Commission will coordinate with Town staff to verify property status. It was also noted that a Regional Planning Commission staff member assisting with mapping for the Master Plan will soon be leaving their position. 3. Prime Wetlands Map update discussion and NH Rule Env-Wt 703.7 – corrections to Prime Wetlands Boundaries The Commission revisited the topic of updating the prime wetlands map.

Chair Crystall had planned to compare the current prime wetlands map (from 1990) and the National Wetlands Inventory (NWI). Mr. O'Donovan noted that while a public hearing is not strictly required, affected landowners must be notified directly if boundaries are reevaluated. Additionally, mapped prime wetland boundaries are considered general, while on-site delineations govern regulatory decisions. Based on these considerations and current workload priorities, Mr. O'Donovan recommended that Conservation Commission Approved Minutes 04/13/2026 3 the Conservation Commission defer any remapping effort at this time.

A related prime wetland discussion arose concerning a recent forestry activity and whether it was in a prime wetland . Differing perspectives were expressed regarding the interpretation of mapping versus field conditions and the role of the Commission in responding to inquiries from state agencies (such as NHDES). Mr. O'Donovan raised concerns about process, communication, and whether the full Commission should have been consulted. The matter highlighted the importance of clear procedures and coordination when addressing potential regulatory issues. 4. Priorities process: Assess, propose, decide, deliver Discussion on this topic was deferred.

Commissioners were encouraged to consider these materials in preparation for future discussions. 5. Land conservation work – status Attention turned to a proposed land donation. Details of the draft agreement were reviewed, including the need to add a lot number and clarify certain provisions. Questions were raised regarding closing costs, which are expected to be modest, and whether the Commission or the Town would be responsible. It was confirmed that the Commission would cover associated costs, with further clarification to be obtained. Ms. Crystall is awaiting a response from the surveyor concerning questions about costs of bounds in addition to the quoted survey cost.

The Commission considered whether to move forward with the draft agreement to the landowner, incorporating suggested edits. A motion was made by Ms. Lindquist and seconded by Mr. Dagavarian to forward the edited Memorandum of Understanding and Gift Agreement to the landowner for donation of Hooksett- Turnpike property. Vote 5:0. It was noted that final approval would require authorization from the Select Board in accordance with statutory requirements. 6. Other (continued) Bow Open Spaces Membership Renewal Mr. O’Donovan recused himself from this topic. A motion was made by Ms. Lindquist and seconded by Ms. Farrell to approve a $1,000 expenditure for the Bow Open Spaces membership renewal.

Vote 4:0:1. Mr. O’Donovan rejoined the meeting. Turee Pond NHDES is holding its annual VLAP (Volunteer Lake Assessment Program) workshop on May 1, 2026 for those interested in conducting sampling. Updates were provided on other administrative and project matters. Upcoming training opportunities and workshops were announced, including a NHACC wetlands-related session. Field work updates included recent easement monitoring in coordination with a state monitoring representative.

Chair Crystall and Charlotte Harding, Program Supervisor - Conservation Land Stewardship Program, walked a few conservation easements including near Bow High School, Conservation Commission Approved Minutes 04/13/2026 4 Briarwood Drive (done by Ms. Harding), off of Birchdale Road, and area near Turee Pond that is accessible from Westgate Drive. Observations included trail conditions, potential unauthorized trail activity (the area near Turee Pond), and the presence of dumped materials (off Birchdale Road), which will require follow-up to determine property boundaries and responsibility. Chair Crystall provided an update on a violation case on Town land where a driveway easement is located.

Chair Crystall noted that the matter is now being addressed with the Pelletier Estate. Chair Crystall discussed the need for greater public engagement, including potential activities tied to community events such as Earth Day, and emphasized the importance of increasing visibility. Financial tracking questions were raised regarding prior expenditures, with follow-up planned once additional detailed information is available. Outreach opportunities were discussed, including sharing information on the NH Turtle Rescue organization regarding seasonal turtle activity. Additional materials from the Saving Special Places conference were made available.

Chair Crystall attended sessions that covered topics such as trail easements, the state wildlife action plan update, and ecosystem reserves. Mr. O'Donovan posed a suggestion about the possibility of making a donation to a state nongame wildlife conservation program. Ms. Crystall will check on whether it is considered a proper use of Commission funds. Mr. O'Donovan raised concerns about a recently installed beaver deceiver and associated site conditions. Mr. O’Donovan recommended that Chair Crystall or someone from the Beaver Subcommittee visit the site to better understand the situation.

The status of the Commission’s beaver management policy was also discussed, with clarification that a draft exists and remains under subcommittee review. Chair Sandy Crystall called the meeting to order at 7:0 2 PM. Commissioners present: Sandy Crystall, Lisa Lindquist, Mary Farrell, Tom O’Donovan , and Dik Dagavarian Other attendees: Ginger Iverson, Recording Secretary 1. River Road Bridge at Bow Bog Brook – Town Wetland Permit Application The Commission first discussed the River Road bridge over Bow Bog Brook project. This bridge is near where Ferry Road splits off of River Road. The Town has received a permit application prepared by Dubois & King, though it ha s not yet been formally presented to the Commission.

The proposed design includes a 28-foot span bridge, which represents a significant increase over the existing 15-foot corrugated metal pipe arch. While the new design improves hydraulic capacity and stream compatibility, it does not fully meet NHDES stream crossing guidelines requiring a span of 1.2 times the bankfull width. Commissioners noted that site constraints may limit compliance but agreed to raise questions with the NH Department of Environmental Services ( NH DES), including clarification on whether the project lies within a wellhead protection or aquifer area. The Commission plans to submit comments once the application is confirmed with NH DES.

Chair Crystall noted that she may adjust the agenda order this evening. 6. Other Planning Board Project Reviews – Loraco Plaza -1494 Route 3-A – Wetland CUP The Commission heard a presentation from Jason Hill of TF Moran and property owner Scott Soucy regarding a proposed commercial development along Route 3 - A. The project entails the construction of two light industrial/flex buildings totaling approximately 8,400 and 3,990 square feet, respectively , with associated parking, drainage, and septic systems. A stormwater management system, previously approved, will be implemented using a bioretention (biofiltration) pond with an underdrain due to high groundwater conditions.

The design includes a discharge pipe and level spreader within the wetland buffer, resulting in temporary and permanent impacts. Commission ers asked about buffer impacts, alternative design options, and the length and placement of the drainage pipe. The applicant explained that site topography, soil conditions, and regulatory setbacks dictated the design. No direct wetland impacts are proposed, and rare species reviews found no concerns. Landscaping plans include mostly native species, though the Commission recommended replacing non-native plantings. Chair Crystall noted that S pir a ea japonica is non-native.

The Commission expects to participate in a site walk with the Planning Board before making a recommendation. 2. Project Reviews Robertson Trail – Seasonal reroute – Permit application update, construction schedule The Commission held a site walk earlier in the day at 4 pm in Knox Forest to review the proposed route and revise as needed. Updates included minor route adjustments, construction details, and materials. The boardwalk /puncheon design will likely use larger lumber (3 ” x 10 ” s instead of 2 ” x 10 ” s) for durability, with no more than one-inch spacing between planks . The total project cost is expected to remain below the budget. Mr.

O'Donovan emphasized the need to finalize construction diagrams for the DES permit application and aim to submit the application by the end of April to allow for late summer construction. Removal of hazardous dead trees along the trail was also supported. Hammond Nature Preserve – Review of current Conservation Restrictions The Commission then revisited the status of the Hammond Nature Preserve and the legal protections governing the land. Mr. O’Donovan noted that Bow Open Spaces believes this property is not effectively protected. A discussion focused on whether the existing conservation restriction provides the same level of protection as a conservation easement.

The T own attorney’s preliminary feedback suggested easements are generally more comprehensive and legally established . The Commissioners agreed to request a legal opinion on whether the current restriction could be altered or removed by T own action . . Survey Boundary Markers on Knox Forest (at Knox Road) There was a brief discussion about verifying boundary markers at Knox Forest and confirming whether bounds are present . Chair Crystall will visit the site to confirm the status of the markers. Master Plan – Conservation Lands Review Ms. Crystall shared the schedule for the upcoming Master Plan subcommittee meeting scheduled for April 23, 2026.

Attendance at the visioning session was noted to be low, particularly for the natural resources sessions . Work related to T own conservation land records is ongoing, including deed research to confirm easements or other restrictions . The Commission will coordinate with Town staff to verify property status . It was also noted that a R egional P lanning Commission staff member assisting with mapping for the Master Plan will soon be leaving their position. 3. Prime Wetlands Map update discussion and NH Rule Env-Wt 703.7 – corrections to Prime Wetlands Boundaries The Commission revisited the topic of updating the prime wetlands map.

Chair Crystall had plan ned to compar e the current prime wetlands map (from 1990) and the National Wetlands Inventory ( NWI ) . Mr. O'Donovan noted that while a public hearing is not strictly required, affected landowners must be notified directly if boundaries are reevaluated. Additionally, mapped prime wetland boundaries are considered general, while on-site delineations govern regulatory decisions. Based on these considerations and current workload priorities, Mr. O'Donovan recommend ed that the Conservation Commission defer any remapping effort at this time. A related prime wetland discussion arose concerning a recent forestry activity and whether it was in a prime wetland .

Differing perspectives were expressed regarding the interpretation of mapping versus field conditions and the role of the Commission in responding to inquiries from state agencies ( s uch as NHDES) . Mr. O'Donovan raised c oncerns about process, communication, and whether the full Commission should have been consulted. The matter highlighted the importance of clear procedures and coordination when addressing potential regulatory issues. 4. Priorities process: Assess, propose, decide, deliver Discussion on this topic was deferred. Commissioners were encouraged to consider these materials in preparation for future discussions. 5.

Land conservation work – status Attention turned to a proposed land donation. Details of the draft agreement were reviewed, including the need to add a lot number and clarify certain provisions. Questions were raised regarding closing costs, which are expected to be modest, and whether the Commission or the Town would be responsible. It was confirmed that the Commission would cover associated costs, with further clarification to be obtained. Ms. Crystall is awaiting a response from the surveyor concerning questions about costs of bounds in addition to the quoted survey cost.

The Commission considered whether to move forward with the draft agreement to the landowner, incorporating suggested edits. A motion was made by Ms. Lindquist and seconded by Mr. Dagavarian to forward the edited Memorandum of Understanding and Gift Agreement to the landowner for donation of Hooksett-Turnpike property . Vote 5:0. It was noted that final approval would require authorization from the Select Board in accordance with statutory requirements. 6. Other (continued) Bow Open Spaces Membership Renewal Mr. O’Donovan recused himself from this topic. A motion was made by Ms. Lindquist and seconded by Ms. Farrell to approve a $1,000 expenditure for the Bow Open Spaces membership renewal.

Vote 4 :0:1 . Mr. Donovan rejoined the meeting. Turee Pond NHDES is holding its annual VLAP (Volunteer Lake Assessment Program) workshop on May 1, 2026 for those interested in conducting sampling . Updates were provided on other administrative and project matters. Upcoming training opportunities and workshops were announced, including a NHA C C wetlands-related session. Field work updates included recent easement monitoring in coordination with a state monitoring representative. Chair Crystall and Charlotte Harding , Program Supervisor - Conservation Land Stewardship Program , walked a fe w conservation easements including near Bow High School, Briarwood Drive (done by Ms.

Harding), off of Birchdale Road , and area near Turee Pond that is accessible from Westgate D rive . Observations included trail conditions, potential unauthorized trail activity (the area near Turee Pond) , and the presence of dumped materials (off Birchdale Road ) , which will require follow-up to determine property boundaries and responsibility. Chair Crystall provided an update on a violation case, noting that the matter is now being addressed through coordination with the property owner’s estate.

Chair Crystall discussed the need for greater public engagement, including potential activities tied to community events such as Earth Day, and emphasized the importance of increasing visibility. Financial tracking questions were raised regarding prior expenditures, with follow-up planned once additional detailed information is available. Outreach opportunities were discussed, including sharing information on the NH Turtle Rescue organization regarding seasonal turtle activity. Additional materials from the Saving Special Places conference were made available .

Chair Crystall attended session s that covered topics such as trail easements , the state wildlife action plan update, and ecosystem reserves. Mr. O'Donovan posed a suggestion about t he possibility of making a donation to a state nongame wildlife conservation program . Ms. Crystall will check on whether it is considered a proper use of Commission funds. Mr. O'Donovan raised c oncerns were raised about a recently installed beaver deceiver and associated site conditions. A site visit was recommended to better understand the situation. The status of the Commission’s beaver management policy was also discussed, with clarification that a draft exists and remains under subcommittee review.

The Commission reviewed and amended prior meeting minutes . Unapproved Minutes: March 16, 2026 M r . Dagavarian made a motion to approve the March 16 , 2026 minutes as amended . The motion was seconded by Ms. Farrell . Vote 5:0 Adjournment Ms. Lindquist made a motion to adjourn the meeting. The motion was seconded by Mr. Dagavarian . Vote 5:0 . The meeting adjourned at 8: 5 0 p.m. Respectfully submitted, Ginger Iverson Recording Secretary

Town of Bow Recycling and Solid Waste Committee Meeting Minutes April 7, 2026 Meeting To: David Stack, Town Manager cc: Bow Administrative Assistant, Committee Webpage, Recycling Committee Members Re : Recycling and Solid Waste Committee Minutes for April 7, 2026 Meeting Date : April 7, 2026 Committee Member Attendees: Sherri Cheney, Heath Carder, Beth Titus, and Irene Hou. Deb Unger attended by phone. Other Attendees: Woody Bowne MEETING BEGAN AT 7:02 P.M. Review of Meeting Minutes Motion by Heath Carder to approve February draft minutes, seconded by Beth Titus, unanimously approved. 2.

Discussion of Paint Legislation Sherri provided a brief overview of New Hampshire HB 451-FN “Paint Product Stewardship Program” which includes both latex and oil based paints. If signed into law, all unused paints would be returned directly to collection sites established by the stewardship program and we would no longer need to accept paint in cans of 5 gallons or less, of any type, at Household Hazardous Waste Day (HHWD). Whil e t his bill passed in both chambers, Governor Ayotte vetoed the legislation . Therefore, we will plan to continue collecting paint at HHWD as per previous years. Grant Closeout Report The annual report was submitted to the town. 4.

Recycling Tipping Fees –Rates Sherri Cheney reported on tipping fees for recyclables. The tipping fee per ton in February was $137.49 and in March was $128.46. 5 . Recycling and Solid Waste Totals Sherri Cheney reported on collection amounts for recycling and solid waste. Single stream recycling was 67.34 tons for January and 51.98 tons for February. Trash was 184.42 tons for January and 152.41 tons in February. 6. Renewal Garden and Compost Update The compost program is running smoothly and is being well used with both totes being filled to least 75% capacity. Monthly fee for collection remain s $124.00 7.

Status of Terra C ycle Containers It was discussed that the collection bins need to be cleaned and flyers need to be updated and repaired. When warm weather arrives, Deb will clean the bins and Irene will update the flyers. It was also discussed that the new bin for drink pouches is not being utilized and incorrect items are being placed in it. Irene will relocate the drink pouch bin next to the squeeze pouch bin and add additional signage to hopefully improve usage and correct separation. Irene volunteered to take over managing the administrative side of the Terra C ycle program.

She placed the request to redeem points which should be just over $400 to be deposited in our account through the Town. 8. Committee Responsibilities and Elections Sherri discussed having elections for the positions of Chair, Vice Chair and Secretary and possibly a Head position to coordinate HHWD. Sherri suggested that if no one wants to take on the role of Chair, we could create a rotating position every 6 months based on seniority within the committee, with Beth Titus for the first 6 months. It was decided that we would make a decision on Chair & Vice Chair at the next meeting when Mark and Taj will hopefully be able to participate. Irene was selected as Secretary.

Deb will be back up Secretary. Sherri also discussed the need to assign specific duties to each member and reviewed the list of duties. Several duties were assigned to committee members as listed below. Unassigned duties will be discussed at the next meeting. Monthly Items: Chair to do agenda Vice Chair to assist Chair and cover when Chair is unavailable Secretary to prepare minutes and send them to town ( Irene;

Deb back up) Member to review weight ships and update numbers on spreadsheet (Beth) Member(s) to empty plastic bins and take plastic to Hannaford (Deb, Beth, Sherri, Leon) Member to check TerraCycle bins, request labels, box and take to UPS (Irene) Member(s) to write Articles for the Bow Times (Beth will write first article for Bow Times) Member to handle social media information (Mark currently has this role) Member to check Committee email and respond to questions (Mark currently has this role) Member to build any additional benches (Heath) Member to review committee information on Town website and work with Tonia on any changes (Irene has already met with Tonia and started the process) Household Hazardous Waste Day jobs:

Annual application for HHW Grant (Irene) Coordination with NH Recycles for HHW date & pricing-or whether to put HHW out for bid Coordinating electronics vendor Coordinating advertising for HHWD Lead position for HHW collection FInal report for HHW collection Additionally, Heath offered to take on some of HHWD coordination, Heath offered to contact Bryce Larrabee to write an article for the Town Crier, and Beth will contact Cindy Klevens, Chair of the Drinking Water Protection Committee, to consider writing an article for the Bow Times regarding the benefits of HHWD for water quality and protection. 9. HOUSEHOLD HAZARDOUS WASTE DAY 2026 The date will be Saturday, October 17, 2026.

Beth Titus will try to remove the “November” sticker on the flyer. Heath will look into another vendor for the flyer if needed. 10. Trex Program: Plastic bag and Film Collection A new rewards program began this year. Each quarter an entry is received for every 250 pounds of plastic collected. At the end of each quarter 25 winners will be drawn and each winner will be allowed to select one of five prizes. Members who collect and deposit Trex recycling will continue to photograph and upload the weights of each collection. 11. HELPSY Residents may schedule curbside pickup of textiles on the HELPSY website at www.helpsy.com.

Pickups are available the second Saturday of each month with a minimum of three bags. Sherri brought up that she may look to set a Helpsy bin at the Bow Rec Center. Next Committee meeting is May 12, 2026 at 7:00 PM. (Moved from May 5 as Sherri will be away.) Meeting adjourned 7:49 p.m. Respectfully Submitted, Irene Hou

Application no. 501-26: Ryan Stacy LLC – Proposed four-lot residential subdivision. 26 Located at 108 River Road; Map 31, Block 5, Lot 21; Zone: Residential One Family (R- 27 1).

28 29 Attorney Maria Dolder and Surveyor Jacques Belanger presented the application on behalf of 30 Ryan Stacy LLC for a four-lot residential subdivision of an 8.39-acre parcel located in the R-1 31 District with frontage on Vaughn Road and River Road. The application was continued from the 32 February meeting to give the applicant time to prepare an erosion and sediment control plan. 33 The applicant presented a drainage report and erosion control notes prepared by Anthony 34 Costello, PE.

35 36 Attorney Dolder explained that a detailed erosion and drainage plan is difficult to prepare for a 37 small subdivision with single-family homes and no new roadway, as house locations and sizes 38 are not yet known. To address the Board’s concerns, a project description and drainage analysis 39 were prepared using reasonable assumptions for pre- and post-development conditions, including 40 the conversion of approximately 14,000 square feet of forested area to 4,000 square feet of 41 impervious surface and 10,000 square feet of grass on each lot.

The erosion control plan focuses 42 on construction best management practices and standard installation details rather than a 43 site-specific layout. Soils on the site were described as well-draining, with most stormwater 44 expected to be contained on site. While some runoff is anticipated along the northern property 45 line, post-development peak flows were found to be negligible and do not warrant stormwater 46 management structures. 47 48 The Board discussed potentially requiring a more detailed, site-specific erosion and sediment 49 control plan as a condition of approval. Mr.

Belanger said that they had prepared something 50 similar on a previous project and he thought it was a reasonable request. These would be lot- 51 specific plans, likely achieved by adding additional details to the septic plans. 52 53 Ms. Crystall questioned the seed mixtures stated on the plans, noting specifically that 54 crownvetch is not a preferred species, as it is invasive. Mr. Belanger stated that they had no 55 problem substituting the seed mix. 56 57 Chair Berube opened the public hearing at 7:08 PM. There being no public comment, he 58 immediately closed the public hearing. 59 60 Mr.

McDaniel inquired about the recommendation from the Drinking Water Protection 61 Committee to require low salt application. The Board determined that it would not be practical 62 to impose the restriction on a residential subdivision with no new roadway. 63 64 Mr. McDaniel also inquired about the staff note regarding certification from a wetlands scientist. 65 Ms. Makinen provided the background information that the applicant provided a note on the plan 66 stating that there are no wetlands on site; however, it is missing the certification of a wetlands 67 scientist. The applicant stated that they had no problem adding that to the final plan.

The snow 68 cover has prevented them from completing that step to date. 69 70 A motion was made by Mr. McDaniel and seconded by Ms. Duke to approve Application #501- 71 26: Ryan Stacy LLC with the following conditions: 72 1. An erosion control plan will be provided for each site prior to the issuance of building 73 permits. 74 2. Crownvetch will be removed from the plan and will not be used for reseeding. 75 3. Address missing checklist items. 76 4. Receipt of state permits. 77 5. Professional stamps and signatures are required on the final plan. 78 6. All waivers granted and conditions of approval shall be noted on the final plan. 79 The Board voted 7:0 in support of the motion. 80 81 Mr.

McDaniel made a motion to approve the following Findings of Fact: 82 1. The proposal is an appropriate use of a residential zone. 83 2. There is no new roadway proposed. 84 The motion was seconded by Ms. Duke and the Board voted unanimously in favor. 85 86 2. Application no. 201-26: Alley Realty, LLC – Change of use site plan to add the use 87 listed in 5.11.C.3: Indoor Commercial Recreational Facility to allow an indoor soccer 88 facility to occupy all four units of the building at 29 Dunklee Road. 89 Located at 29 Dunklee Road; Map 35, Block 2, Lot 162-A; Zone: General Industrial (I- 90 2). 91 92 Chair Berube read the application into the record.

93 94 Shaun Blay of Samba Street, LLC and Andrew MacLaren and Ron MacLaren, Jr. of Alley 95 Realty introduced themselves and presented the application. Mr. Blay explained that they would 96 be renting all four units of the building at 29 Dunklee, the second of four approved buildings in 97 the development. Most of the floor area would comprise of a turf field, sized for 7 v. 7 play, 98 with bathrooms and a check-in area. The facility would be used for training and player 99 development with 20-24 youth and a few coaches using it at a time. Due to the restrictions of a 100 smaller field size, they would not be renting the facility to teams or leagues.

101 102 The parking regulations require 42 parking spaces based on 1 space per 200 square feet of 103 gymnasium floor area. The category for gymnasium isn’t a perfect match for the soccer field, 104 but it is the best option available. There will be no spectator seating. The applicant has provided 105 39 parking spaces, which includes 15 proposed spaces that were not marked on the original site 106 plan. 107 108 Ms. Duke made a motion, seconded by Ms. Crystall, that the application is complete. The Board 109 voted unanimously in favor. 110 111 Ms. Makinen pointed out the location of the proposed parking spaces on plan, noting that they 112 are on the pervious pavement.

The Board discussed and came to a consensus that the location 113 was appropriate, but that salt and sand should not be used on the pervious pavement. 114 115 Chair Berube opened and then closed a public hearing at 7:22 PM, as there were no members of 116 the public wishing to speak. 117 118 The Board discussed potential conditions of approval, including that the use should remain one 119 field across all four units of the building. If the building was broken up into separate indoor 120 recreation uses in the future, the parking requirements could be drastically different.

121 Additionally, the Board discussed limiting the use to not allow tournaments or other large events, 122 but it was determined to not be necessary or practical. 123 124 Mr. Blay noted that there would be active entrances/exits at both the front and rear of the 125 building, so the parking can be utilized equally on both sides. 126 127 Mr. McDaniel made a motion that the application does not have regional impact. Ms. Duke 128 seconded the motion, followed by a unanimous vote in favor. 129 130 Mr. McDaniel made a motion to approve a parking waiver, allowing 39 parking spaces where 42 131 are required by the Site Plan Regulations.

The waiver is justified by the fact that the number of 132 spaces provided is extremely close to the standard and the nature of the building suggests that 133 the parking will be sufficient based on the business plan proposed. In addition, the Town’s 134 parking standard is based off a generic gymnasium category, which is a little different from the 135 proposed use. The motion was seconded by Ms. Duke and the Board voted unanimously in favor. 136 137 A motion was made by Mr. McDaniel and seconded by Ms. Duke to approve Application #201- 138 26: Alley Realty, LLC with the following conditions: 139 1. The building shall remain a single field across all four units of the building. 140 2.

There will be active front and rear doors on the facility. 141 3. Record a signed Notice of Decision at the Merrimack County Registry of Deeds. 142 4. All original conditions of approval remain in effect. 143 The Board voted unanimously in favor. 144 145 Mr. McDaniel made a motion for Findings of Fact: 146 1. It is an appropriate use of the building based on the local zoning. 147 2. The Town’s parking regulations would categorize the use as a gymnasium, but it’s not an 148 exact match. 149 3. The proposal is to rent all four units of the building, meaning that they are not competing 150 for parking with other tenants. 151 152 The motion was seconded by Ms.

Duke and all Board members voted in favor. 153 154 III NEW BUSINESS 155 156 IV OLD BUSINESS 157 158 Ms. Makinen reminded the Board of the upcoming Master Plan Community Visioning Session 159 on Wednesday, March 25 at 6:30 PM at the Bow High School auditorium. Pizza and childcare 160 will be provided. There will be five breakout sessions on various topics with Central NH 161 Regional Planning Commission staff and Master Plan Steering Committee members facilitating 162 discussions. Planning Board members are encouraged to participate and help spread the word. 163 164 V CORRESPONDENCE AND OTHER BUSINESS 165 166 Chair Berube asked about the status of the development at 12 Logging Hill Road.

There is a sign 167 up on the property and a lot of discussion on Facebook. Ms. Makinen explained that the Town 168 has not yet received a plan, but expects that there will be Conceptual Consultation soon. 169 170 Ms. Makinen also explained that there are a number of applications in the works for the 171 upcoming Planning Board meetings. She plans to be here for the April meeting, but will be on 172 maternity leave for the May and June meetings. While she is out, Matt Monahan of the Central 173 NH Regional Planning Commission will provide circuit rider assistance to the Board. 174 175 The new Land Use Assistant in the Community Development Department will begin work on 176 March 30.

177 178 Ms. Duke asked about local regulation of logging and the Town’s approval of an Intent to Cut. 179 Ms. Crystall and Ms. Makinen responded by explaining that towns are unable to regulate logging 180 and the Intent to Cut is really a tax document for the NH Department of Revenue Administration 181 (DRA). The Town is required to sign it unless very specific criteria are not met. 182 183 VI REVIEW OF MINUTES 184 185 The Board reviewed the minutes from the February 19, 2026 Planning Board meeting. 186 187 A motion was made by Mr. McDaniel and seconded by Ms. Duke to approve the minutes of 188 February 19, 2026. The motion passed with a unanimous vote in favor.
189 190 VII NON-PUBLIC SESSION RSA 91-A:3 191 192 Mr. McDaniel made a motion to adjourn at 7:34 PM. Ms. Duke seconded the motion. The 193 Planning Board unanimously voted in favor. 194

Due to the restrictions of a 100 smaller field size, they would not be renting the facility to teams or leagues.

101 102 The parking regulations require 42 parking spaces based on 1 space per 200 square feet of 103 gymnasium floor area. The category for gymnasium isn’t a perfect match for the soccer field, 104 but it is the best option available. There will be no spectator seating. The applicant has provided 105 39 parking spaces, which includes 15 proposed spaces that were not marked on the original site 106 plan. 107 108 Ms. Duke made a motion, seconded by Ms. Crystall, that the application is complete. The Board 109 voted unanimously in favor. 110 111 Ms. Makinen pointed out the location of the proposed parking spaces on plan, noting that they 112 are on the pervious pavement.

The Board discussed and came to a consensus that the location 113 was appropriate, but that salt and sand should not be used on the pervious pavement. 114 115 Chair Berube opened and then closed a public hearing at 7:22 PM, as there were no members of 116 the public wishing to speak. 117 118 The Board discussed potential conditions of approval, including that the use should remain one 119 field across all four units of the building. If the building were broken up into separate indoor 120 recreation uses in the future, the parking requirements could be drastically different.

121 Additionally, the Board discussed limiting the use to not allow tournaments or other large events, 122 but it was determined to not be necessary or practical. 123 124 Mr. Blay noted that there would be active entrances/exits at both the front and rear of the 125 building, so the parking can be utilized equally on both sides. 126 127 Mr. McDaniel made a motion that the application does not have regional impact. Ms. Duke 128 seconded the motion, followed by a unanimous vote in favor. 129 130 Mr. McDaniel made a motion to approve a parking waiver, allowing 39 parking spaces where 42 131 are required by the Site Plan Regulations.

The waiver is justified by the fact that the number of 132 spaces provided is extremely close to the standard and the nature of the building suggests that 133 the parking will be sufficient based on the business plan proposed. In addition, the Town’s 134 parking standard is based off a generic gymnasium category, which is a little different from the 135 proposed use. The motion was seconded by Ms. Duke and the Board voted unanimously in favor. 136 137 A motion was made by Mr. McDaniel and seconded by Ms. Duke to approve Application #201- 138 26: Alley Realty, LLC with the following conditions: 139 1. The building shall remain a single field across all four units of the building. 140 2.

There will be active front and rear doors on the facility. 141 3. Record a signed Notice of Decision at the Merrimack County Registry of Deeds. 142 4. All original conditions of approval remain in effect. 143 The Board voted unanimously in favor. 144 145 Mr. McDaniel made a motion for Findings of Fact: 146 1. It is an appropriate use of the building based on the local zoning. 147 2. The Town’s parking regulations would categorize the use as a gymnasium, but it’s not an 148 exact match. 149 3. The proposal is to rent all four units of the building, meaning that they are not competing 150 for parking with other tenants. 151 152 The motion was seconded by Ms.

Duke and all Board members voted in favor. 153 154 III NEW BUSINESS 155 156 IV OLD BUSINESS 157 158 Ms. Makinen reminded the Board of the upcoming Master Plan Community Visioning Session 159 on Wednesday, March 25 at 6:30 PM at the Bow High School auditorium. There will be five breakout sessions on various topics with Central NH 161 Regional Planning Commission staff and Master Plan Steering Committee members facilitating 162 discussions. Planning Board members are encouraged to participate and help spread the word. 163 164 V CORRESPONDENCE AND OTHER BUSINESS 165 166 Chair Berube asked about the status of the development at 12 Logging Hill Road.

There is a sign 167 up on the property and a lot of discussion on Facebook. Ms. Makinen explained that the Town 168 has not yet received a plan, but expects that there will be Conceptual Consultation soon. 169 170 Ms. Makinen also explained that there are a number of applications in the works for the 171 upcoming Planning Board meetings. She plans to be here for the April meeting, but will be on 172 maternity leave for the May and June meetings. While she is out, Matt Monahan of the Central 173 NH Regional Planning Commission will provide circuit rider assistance to the Board. 174 175 The new Land Use Assistant in the Community Development Department will begin work on 176 March 30.

BOW HERITAGE COMMISSION March 17th, 2026 MEETING MINUTES Call to order: 9am Public comment - Dick Stevens is slowly unpacking treasures. He brought political pins with him to share with the BHC. This is a great opportunity to showcase some items. GUESTS/VOLUNTEERS - Janet Shaw, Kay Herrick, Dick & Alna Stevens, Candy Ricard & Chris Andrews. GENERAL BUSINESS - Attendance - Eric Anderson,Chair; Sue Wheeler, Secretary; Dik Dagavarian, Treasurer; Jim Dimick, John Urdi, Don Fournier, Dave West and Dave Lindquist. Absent is Eleana Colby, Select Board representative. Minutes - February 10th, and February 27th, 2026. Don moves the 2/10/26 minutes with Jim seconding the motion.

No further discussion, and the Ayes have it, 8 to 0. John moves the 2/27/26 minutes with Jim seconding the motion. Upon further discussion, John finds the minutes muddled. Sue agrees and will check with Cheryl about some clarification. Ayes have it, 7 to 0, with 1 abstention. BHC Financials - The operating budget balance is $575.00, with $45.00 spent in February for lunch at the NH Preservation Alliance workshop that Eric, John and Dave West attended. The Heritage Fund balance is $24,614.39 with $70.84 in interest income and $20.00 of merchandise income. These numbers were not available for the meeting and thus were not approved. The figures came by email for recording purposes only.

We shall approve these figures in the April meeting. BHC Appropriation - These are the costs of display materials for 2 exhibit towers. Inkjet paper 50 sheets 8.5 x 11 inches = $40.00 Inkjet paper 50 sheets 13 x 19 inches = $100.00 Inkjet ink, 1 pkg. of 10 cartridges =$130.00 16 Frames 13x19 inches at $15.00 each = $240.00 32 Frames 8.5 x 11 inches at $16.00 each = $192.00 Total Cost = $702.00 We need one or two people to select the photos. John makes a motion to expend up to $740.00 for materials for the towers. Dik seconds the motion. No further discussion, and the Ayes have it, 8 to 0. Motion passes. Eric praises John and the crew for the construction of the display towers. Dave L.

asks if we need to acquire additional wires or brackets to display other than photos? How will it work? Additional money would come out of the HF fund unless we wait until July 1st. A Preservation Newsletter was picked up at our mailbox and a notice for the Old House and Barn expo.

OLD BUSINESS - Chris Andrews - Building and advisory committee update… Tonight the committee meets (3/17/26) and the BBMH is on the agenda. Dave W. says at least the minimum talked about tonight should be basic maintenance. The Capital Reserve budget starts right now. At the Town meeting it was suggested by the BoS to “fundraise” for expenses. No other town owned building that we know of has to fundraise to get basic maintenance done. When they had suggested fundraising, maybe they were confused with the carriage shed proposal from before. Chris uses a spreadsheet that the $60,000.00 for painting and clapboard repair is the set price for now.

Depending on what year, he allows approximately 3.5% increase for each year forward for when the work is to be done. The final report goes to the CIP. Dave W. asks Chris if he will suggest this as a priority? Yes. Chris asks if there is rumor about another plan that doesn’t include the carriage sheds? Eric states that the BHC has been working on a suitable plan for 5-7 years or more. Jim then suggests his idea for an addition in the back of the BBMH. We need to set up an informational meeting with the Bos to network a plan.

But unfortunately the expanding of the meetinghouse doesn’t seem relevant now.( The Select Board has only been complaining about such limited revenue from the buildings rental ideas for 20 plus years) Janet says the BHC had a wonderful idea to add on to the BBMH to celebrate the 300th Anniversary of the Town. Dik then explains that the proposal went before the Building Advisory committee and the CIP but the dollar amount was too much to agree upon.(This total amount also included a large sum of money to fix around the steeple for water leaking in. Upon a second opinion by Steve Fifield, that was NOT correct). The Town just didn’t like the idea. Period.

Dick Stevens agrees with Janet Shaw that the carriage sheds were ideal without the aesthetics being disturbed. Eric says the direction of the BoS is different. They wanted expanded use, now maintain w/o money to spend. Chris suggests asking some of these different proposals before the Select Board as “What do they see in the future?” Preferably a work session before a BoS meeting? What is their suggestion? Kay read recently that the Warner Church is upgrading their building to become a community center and food pantry to have more exposure for all. Towns are definitely different. Dave W. asks if an alarm system is feasible for the BBMH? Chris will address this in due time.

A basic system would work. Line item for next year? We hope so. Chris asks us about lighting downstairs in the BHC headquarters? Unitil has expanded the LED replacement program. He wants us to think about lights such as in a museum. Between now and May he is working with a lighting consultant. They are a private company that fulfill schools, Town offices, etc. They come in, suggest and install. There will be money available up until the end of December. Chris will see him tomorrow and see if he’s available to meet with us on the 24th of March after morning, perhaps 1 pm?

TOWN OF BOW Conservation Commission 10 Grandview Road, Bow, New Hampshire 03304 Phone (603) 223-3970 Fax (603) 225-2982 Website: www.bownh.gov Email: conservation@bownh.gov Conservation Commission Approved Minutes Monday, February 9, 2026 The regular meeting of the Bow Conservation Commission was held on Monday, February 9, 2026 at 7:00 PM in Room C of the Municipal Office building at 10 Grandview Road. Chair Sandy Crystall called the meeting to order at 7:00 PM. Commissioners present: Sandy Crystall, Lisa Lindquist, Mary Farrell, and Tom O’Donovan (via telephone). Excused: Dik Dagavarian Other attendees: Ginger Iverson, Recording Secretary. Mr.

O’Donovan stated that he could not attend the meeting in person as he was out of town. The Commission permitted Mr. O’Donovan to participate remotely, as he was out of town, in accordance with RSA 91-A:2, III. A quorum was confirmed with members physically present. 1. Town Culvert – Bow Bog Brook/Bow Bog Road Chris Albert, Wetland Scientist retained by the Town of Bow provided an informational overview of the proposed replacement of the existing culvert on Bow Bog Brook where it crosses South Bow Road. He noted that this was informational only; formal plans are not yet complete. Mr. Albert described the existing structure is a 4-foot diameter corrugated metal pipe (CMP) that is undersized.

Ms. Crystall noted that it is a 15-foot-wide stream. The CMP is deteriorating, with corrosion and failing rivets. The project was previously submitted for ARM Fund funding (2023), but funding was not secured at that time. A key challenge was confirmation of the roadway right-of- way (ROW); survey work confirmed a four-rod (66-foot) right-of-way, allowing the project to remain fully within the Town ROW. The proposed design includes replacement with a precast concrete box culvert, approximately 8 feet wide by 6 feet deep (construction height) by 50 feet long. It will have 4 feet of hydraulic opening with 2 feet of streambed simulation.

The new structure would triple hydraulic capacity compared to the existing CMP. Streambed simulation will mimic natural conditions and improve aquatic organism passage (AOP). Shelving will be incorporated to allow turtles and other wildlife to pass through the culvert above the water without crossing the road. The design addresses Blanding’s turtle and wood turtle habitat concerns, identified in NHB data checks (DES Ecological review.) Guardrails (approximately 75 feet on each side) are included for public safety. Conservation Commission Approved Minutes 02/09/2026 2 Mr.

Albert stated that because the road was never overtopped by flooding and it had freeboard the hope is that DES may waive certain requirements. The FEMA flood map displayed depicted that the road is not overtopped during a 100-year flood. Construction Considerations - Target construction window: August 2026, during low-flow conditions. Road closure during construction is likely, similar to a previous culvert project in Town, hence completing the construction when school is not in session is preferred. Bypass flow options were discussed; a cofferdam and pump system may be required if the stream is not dry at the time of construction.

Permitting and Schedule - A DES pre-application meeting is scheduled with Kara Villone, the wetlands permitting specialist. The project will be included as a warrant article at Town Meeting. If approved, bidding would occur in spring 2026, with construction later in the summer. Cost Estimate - Total estimated project cost: approximately $400,000, including ~$65,000 for the precast box culvert ~ $150,000 for installation. Other costs include traffic control, guardrails, engineering, permitting, and contingency. Ms. Crystall noted that the previous design described in the ARM Fund application was significantly higher, $900,000, so this is a significantly lower cost project.

The Conservation Commission expressed strong support for the project. The Commission indicated willingness to speak in favor of the warrant article if questions arise at Town Meeting. No formal action was required at this time, as the presentation was informational only. 2. S3AK Lot 27-3-30-I at South Bow Road; Weland CUP for 2,866 sq. ft. of wetlands and 11.797 sq. ft. of wetland buffer impacts for a driveway. The Commission discussed concerns related to a Conditional Use Permit application previously reviewed by the Planning Board and Conservation Commission. The applicant was not present at this meeting. The Key Issues Identified were: 1.

Applicant Absence o No representative was present to answer Commission questions, limiting the Commission’s ability to complete its review. 2. Inaccuracies in the CUP Narrative Document o The narrative incorrectly states that the Conservation Commission had recommended approval. o Errors were noted regarding use of term wetland “functions” versus “values.” o Statements regarding minimizing impacts were inconsistent with the data presented. 3. Land Ownership Information o The site plan lists incorrect landowner name and must be corrected. 4. Current Use Status o The application indicates the property is in current use/open space.

o A question was raised about the status l as it does not appear on the most recent Current Use listing. Conservation Commission Approved Minutes 02/09/2026 3 o Staff will verify the property’s current use status. 5. Wetland Buffer Impacts o The narrative references approximately 2,900 square feet of wetland impact but fails to adequately acknowledge over 11,000 square feet of wetland buffer impact (12.05 F). o Members expressed concern that buffer impacts were minimized despite their ecological importance. 6. NHB (Natural Heritage Bureau) /DES Ecological Review o The map included “notification points” (red dots) which represent areas where work will be undertaken.

The Data check appears to be for the timber harvesting, not driveway construction. o The Commission requested clarification from DES regarding the meaning of these points and whether additional ecological review is required. Mr. O’Donovan made a motion to forward the Commission’s concerns to the Planning Board. The motion was seconded by Lisa Lindquist. The motion was approved by 3:0:1 roll call vote. Lisa Lindquist – Yes; Tom O’Donovan – Yes; Mary Farrell – Yes; Sandy Crystall – Abstained 3. Master Plan Update Members discussed the recent Master Plan meeting that focused on transportation.

Survey results indicated strong public concern for protection of natural resources, salt contamination of groundwater and preservation of rural and open-space character. Members noted these results may indicate support for future conservation and buffer-related policies. The next Master Plan meeting is scheduled for February 17, 2026. The Commission anticipates reviewing the Natural Resources chapter later in the year and may begin internal discussions in advance. 4. Land Conservation Work – Non-Public Session – RSA 91-A:3, II Mr. O’Donovan made a motion, seconded by Ms.

Farrell, to enter non-public session per RSA 91-A:3, II (d) Consideration of the acquisition, sale or lease of real or personal property which, if discussed in public would likely benefit a party or parties whose interests are adverse to those of the general community. 4:0 Roll Call Vote: Lisa Lindquist – Yes; Tom O’Donovan – Yes; Mary Farrell – Yes; Sandy Crystall – Yes Recording was turned off at 8:12 p.m. and entered into non-public session. Public Session was reconvened at 8:26 p.m. Ms. Lindquist made a motion to seal the non-public minutes per RSA 91-A:3, II. Motion was seconded by Ms. Farrell. 4:0 Roll Call Vote: Lisa Lindquist – Yes; Tom O’Donovan – Yes; Mary Farrell – Yes;

Sandy Crystall – Yes 5. Website Review and Updates The Commission reviewed its website and associated documents. Conservation Commission Approved Minutes 02/09/2026 4 Several broken links were identified, largely due to changes to the Bow Open Spaces website. Documents reviewed included trail maps, conservation documents, the Bow Master Plan (Natural Resources chapter), and open space materials. The Open Space Trails Plan (dated 2000) was noted as outdated and in need of review due to changes in trail use, and land management practices. The Prime Wetlands Map was discussed; members noted it is difficult to read and that the location of the original hard copy map is unknown.

The Timber Cruise / Forest Management Plan (last updated in 2011) was discussed, with consensus that it needs updating and may require a new approach reflecting current forest management philosophies. The State Wildlife Action Plan link was noted as needing an update, as the 2025 plan was just released. The Town Forest Map (2011) was reviewed; members noted that while conservation land has been added, not all parcels are designated as town forest. The “View All” button on the website was discussed; members agreed to review design limitations at a future meeting. Ginger will coordinate with Karri to update broken links and images on the website.

The Commission will review options for updating forest management and stewardship planning. Website graphics and the Commission group photo will be updated. The Commission discussed the need to explore forest management plans that are not strictly timber focused. They recognize that the existing plan was developed under assumptions of more frequent logging, which may no longer align with current goals. Town conservation lands need stewardship plans The Westover easement was noted as having an existing stewardship plan due to state permitting requirements. 6. Project Review Table The project review table was discussed.

Members agreed it is helpful but should be improved to allow sorting by priorities and dates. The table is serving as a useful tool for identifying ongoing and future Commission work. Robinson Trail Project The functional assessment for the Robinson Trail was received today, within the required 30-day period. Next steps include preparing and submitting the DES application and associated plans. The need for potential waiver requests was discussed due to unstamped plan elements, among other requirements. Sandy will continue plan development and coordinate as needed. Mr. O’Donovan departed the meeting at 8:45 p.m.

Legislative Update Commissioners discussed pending legislation related to land placed in Current Use. House Bill 1691 was described as highly restrictive and problematic. Commissioners were encouraged to submit comments before the deadline. Prime Wetlands Map Update Sandy reported discussions with a wetland scientist regarding updating the Prime Wetlands Map, as he has updated prime wetlands maps for two other communities. Preliminary cost estimates indicate the update could be completed for under $10,000, potentially avoiding the need for an RFP.

Conservation Commission Approved Minutes 02/09/2026 5 The process for submitting updated maps and a report to meet DES requirements remains unclear; additional clarification is pending. The Commission should request a formal proposal for Prime Wetlands Map update for review at a future meeting. 7. Other Water Quality Monitoring (Turee Pond) The DES contract for milfoil removal by diver-assisted suction harvesting has been signed and will be provided to DES for Executive Council approval. Volunteers may be needed to assist with monthly summer sampling (June, July and August). Sampling requires two people; having volunteers with their own canoe or kayak is preferred.

Conferences, Training, and Outreach Commissioners were invited to suggest topics for the NHACC Conference or future lunch-and-learn sessions. The Merrimack River Watershed Conservation Plan and DES Ecological Review process were suggested as potential presentation topics. The UNH Coverts Program is seeking applicants. Unapproved Minutes: January 12, 2026 Mr. Lindquist made a motion to approve the January 12, 2026 minutes as amended. The motion was seconded by Ms. Farrell. 3:0 Vote. Adjournment Ms. Lindquist made a motion to adjourn the meeting. The motion was seconded by Ms. Farrell. 3:0 Vote. The meeting adjourned at 8:59 p.m. Respectfully submitted, Ginger Iverson Recording Secretary

(By Petition) New Hampshire communities value strong public schools and responsible use of public funds for education. Therefore, the voters of Bow, New Hampshire, are asked: Shall we call on our legislators to protect taxpayers by requiring the Education Freedom Account program to provide fiscal and educational performance reports comparable to those required of public schools, and by limiting eligibility to families with demonstrated financial need?

This question is raised because state legislators recently removed all income limits from the Education Freedom Account program (vouchers), expanding it beyond its original purpose. These changes added tens of millions of dollars in costs while the program provides limited public information on how funds are spent or if educational standards are being met. The voucher program is projected to cost $110 million over the next two years, with no new revenue sources identified. This directs public funds to private education without reducing the expenses public schools are constitutionally required to cover, increasing pressure on local property taxes.

Committee members in attendance : Chair Lisa Franklin, Vice Chair Jeff Knight, Selectman Chris Nicolopoulos, William Knapp, Martin Osterloh, Melynie Klunk, Mike Mayo, Andrew Mattiace , and Ben Davis. Absent (excused): None. Public Present : Jeff Craig , Kara Smith, Randy and Lori Robertson, Bob Arnold, Van Mosher, Seth Pingree, Eric Anderson, Michael Wheeler, Monica Swenson, Sarah Olson, Nate Haskell, Joe Rider, Cathy Knowles, Judson Malone , Mike Habib , Jenna Reardon and Angela Hubbard , Bow Town employees and Bow school employees. BUDGET COMMITTEE PUBLIC HEARING Call to Order - Chair Lisa Franklin opened the public hearing at 6: 18 PM. All stood and recited the Pledge of Allegiance.

Budget Presentation (Handouts Provided) P roposed Town Budget - Chair Franklin gave a summary of the Town budget . The proposed budget is an increase of $3,224,069 from the approved 2025-26 budget but there is an increase in revenues of $2,838,710 due in part from an increase in motor vehicle fees. Once net appropriations and overlay are added in, the proposed 2026-27 budget is “flat ” with the same municipal tax rate as the previous year of $4.62 or 0% increase . Chair Franklin opened the discussion for questions. There were no questions. Selectman Nicolopoulos then spoke to the Warrant Articles .

Warrant Article #3 – The Town of Bow recently learned they would qualify for $2 million dollars in grants to be applied to an exten tion of the waterline from the Concord City Limits to Bow Junction (Dunkin Donuts south to intersection, left at the intersection up to the wastewater plant on Hall Street). Any money in excess of the grant amount would come from the Bow Business Corridor Tax Increment Financing District Fund. If, in the future, Concord did agree to interconnect with Bow all the steps needed to implement the water line extension would occur with zero impact on the tax base. The remaining Warrant Article s #4 – 16 were presented by Selectman Nicolopolous.

The Chair called for questions. Sensing none, Chair Franklin closed the Town portion of the hearing Proposed 2026-27 Bow School Budget – Chair Franklin opened the School Budget portion of the public hearing and gave an overview of the proposed 2026-27 school budget. The Budget Committee met with the School Department several times . The first budget presented included an 8.37% increase from the approved 2025/26 one. The Committee asked the school department to come back and present a tiered list of reductions to their proposed budget . Chair Franklin referred the taxpayers to the packet provided for this hearing for additional information.

Costs driving the budget include S alaries and Benefits, and Contracted Services. The school proposes a 4% cost-of-living increase, most of which has been negotiated under contract and collective bargaining agreements. Health insurance costs ha d a n increase of 16% . Contracted services have increased 11% due in large part to special education transportation costs. The School Board agreed to lower their contribution to their capital improvement plan from $1,000,000 to $ 7 0 0,000 to balance the impact of increased health care costs . The School Board has made several cuts but at some point, cuts start to impact on student services. Warrant Articles #2 - #12 were reviewed.
